text: Scientists put [[fossil|fossil]] feathers under super-powerful [[@microscopes|microscopes]] and found tiny colour packets called [[melanosome|melanosomes]].
Their shape is the clue. Round packets make ginger-brown. Long, thin packets make black or grey. No packets means white.

That's how we know little Sinosauropteryx had a ginger-and-white striped tail, a bit like a [[@red-panda|red panda]]. For most dinosaurs, though, no colour clues survive, so the colours in books are still an artist's best guess.

quiz.prompt: Many dinosaurs with colour clues were darker on top and paler underneath. Why might that be?

options.t: It helped them hide, by cancelling out shadows
Their bellies faded from lying in the sun
Dark backs kept the rain off

quiz.reveal: This pattern is called countershading. Sunlight from above makes a belly look shadowy, so a pale belly evens things out and the animal looks flatter and harder to see. Deer, sharks and many birds use the same trick today.

src: Zhang F. et al. (2010) Fossilized melanosomes and the colour of Cretaceous dinosaurs and birds. Nature 463.
Vinther J. (2015) A guide to the field of palaeo colour. BioEssays 37.
n.certNote: We know the colours of only a few dinosaurs with well-preserved feathers. Most colours in pictures are guesses.

d.try: Shine a torch from above onto a ball. The bottom looks dark. Now colour the bottom half of the ball (or a paper cup) a lighter shade and the top half darker, and shine the torch again. From a distance, the shading almost disappears. That's countershading.
myth: Dinosaurs were green or grey, like lizards and elephants.
For most dinosaurs, we simply don't know. The few with colour clues were ginger, black, white, brown or shimmering, and many had stripes, masks or pale bellies.

sec.t:
Melanosomes are far too small to see with an ordinary [[microscope|microscope]]. They are made of [[melanin|melanin]], the same pigment that colours your hair and skin. In 2008, a scientist studying fossil feathers noticed that tiny shapes once thought to be bacteria matched melanosomes in living birds.

In 2010, two teams used this idea on dinosaurs for the first time. They compared the shapes in fossils with those in modern bird feathers, where the colours are known. Matching the shapes told them the colours. It is a bit like recognising [[@words-handwriting|a friend's handwriting]]. You don't need to see them write, because the shapes of the letters give them away. The fossils have to be special, though. They must come from very fine mud or volcanic ash, where feathers were pressed flat and sealed away from air.

Colours can also tell us how dinosaurs lived. Psittacosaurus, a small horned dinosaur from China, was darker on top and paler underneath. Scientists even built a model and lit it to test the pattern. It matched animals that live in shady forests.

In 2017, a heavily armoured dinosaur from Alberta, Canada, called Borealopelta, was found with its skin preserved. It was reddish-brown on top and lighter below. An animal as big and armoured as a small tank still needed to [[@camouflage|hide]], which tells us its [[predator|predators]] must have been fearsome. A [[@tiger-stripes|tiger's stripes]] work in a similar way, helping it vanish in long grass.

Melanosomes only tell part of the story. Many birds get their bright reds and yellows from [[pigment|pigments]] in their food, such as the pink of a flamingo. Those pigments break down much more easily and are rarely found in fossils. Blues and greens in birds often come from the structure of the feather rather than pigment, and are hard to detect.

So a dinosaur might have had bright patches we can't see. Some scientists also argue that a few of the tiny shapes could still be [[bacteria|bacteria]], so they check each case carefully.

Colour is one of the hardest parts of an animal to rebuild from fossils. Bones give the shape, but the outside is usually guesswork. Every real colour clue helps artists and scientists make better pictures, and shows which parts of a [[@how-reconstruct|reconstruction]] are evidence and which are imagination. Some living animals, like the [[@octopus-smart|octopus]], can change colour in a blink. For dinosaurs, we are still finding out what colours they wore at all.

text: Most dinosaurs were probably no faster than today's big animals, and the giants were fairly slow. Small two-legged dinosaurs were the speed champions. Some footprint trails show them moving at around 40 km/h, as fast as a [[@body-speed-limit|top human sprinter]].

Scientists work out speeds in two ways. [[fossil|Fossil]] footprints show how a real animal moved on a real day. [[@computers-how|Computer models]] of skeletons and [[@muscles|muscles]] test how fast a body could go. The two often disagree for big, famous dinosaurs like T. rex, which is why the question is still argued about.

st.prompt: In the film Jurassic Park, a T. rex chases a speeding jeep. What do most scientists think?

options.t: A real T. rex could not keep up with a car going 50 km/h
A real T. rex was even faster than the film shows
A real T. rex could not walk at all

st.reveal: Computer models suggest a grown T. rex was too heavy to sprint. Its leg bones and muscles would not cope with the forces. Most estimates put its top speed somewhere between a fast jog and a sprinter's pace.

src: Alexander R.McN. (1976) Estimates of speeds of dinosaurs. Nature 261.
Hutchinson J.R. and Garcia M. (2002) Tyrannosaurus was not a fast runner. Nature 415.
n.certNote: Speeds worked out from footprints are fairly reliable for the animals that made them. Top speeds for famous dinosaurs like T. rex come from computer models, and different models give different answers.

d.try: In a playground, walk ten steps and measure the distance between your footprints or chalk marks. Then jog ten steps and measure again. Your steps get longer as you go faster. That's the same clue scientists use with dinosaur tracks.
myth: T. rex could chase down a speeding car.
Studies of its leg muscles and bones suggest an adult T. rex could not sprint. Most estimates are below 40 km/h, and some are as low as a brisk walk or slow jog.
facts: spacing of footprints, and computer models

sec.t:
In 1976, a British zoologist called Robert McNeill Alexander found a simple rule. He studied living animals, from people to elephants. When any animal speeds up, its stride gets longer compared to its leg length. So if you know the length of a dinosaur's leg and the gap between its [[@dino-feet-tracks|footprints]], you can estimate its [[@speed-distance|speed]].

Leg length can be worked out from the size of the footprint itself. Using this rule, scientists have measured thousands of trackways around the world.

The rule has limits. Very soft mud can stretch or smear prints, and an animal that slipped or turned changed its stride. So scientists look for long, straight trails with clear prints. Even then, they give a range of speeds rather than one exact number, because a leg length worked out from a footprint is itself an estimate.

Some trackways do show running. In 2021, scientists in La Rioja, Spain, described tracks left by two-legged meat-eaters with very long strides. One worked out at about 45 km/h, nearly as fast as the Olympic sprinter [[@usain-bolt|Usain Bolt]] at full speed.

Ornithomimids, often called "ostrich mimic" dinosaurs, had long slim legs, light bodies and big thigh muscles. Many scientists think they were among the fastest dinosaurs. The ostrich itself, a [[@birds-dinosaurs|living dinosaur]], can reach about 70 km/h.

For T. rex, there are no running tracks to measure, so scientists build computer models. In 2002, John Hutchinson and Mariano Garcia worked out how much leg muscle T. rex would need to run fast. A sprinting T. rex would have needed far more than its legs could hold.

Later models gave a range of answers. Some suggest a top speed of about 25–40 km/h. One study in 2017 argued its bones would have broken at any pace faster than a brisk walk of about 20 km/h. Big animals face a real limit. Weight grows faster than the strength of bones and muscles, which is why elephants never gallop.

Young T. rex were slimmer, with longer legs for their size. They may have been the quick ones, chasing fast prey that their heavy parents could not catch. Growing up, a T. rex may have swapped speed for size and strength.

text: A hot spring is a place where warm or hot water flows out of the ground. It starts as ordinary rain or snow that soaks down through cracks in the rock. Deep underground, the rock is hot, and the water heats up. Hot water is lighter than cold water, so it rises back to the surface through other cracks.

In some places the heat comes from [[magma|magma]], molten rock not far below the surface, as at Yellowstone in the USA or in Iceland. In others the water simply sinks very deep, because the Earth gets hotter the further down you go, roughly 25–30 °C warmer for every kilometre.
A geyser is a special kind of hot spring that erupts, shooting water and steam into the air every so often.

st.prompt: Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone has rings of orange, yellow and green around a blue centre. What makes the colours?

options.t: Different microbes that like different temperatures

st.reveal: The centre is too hot for most life and looks deep blue. As the water flows outwards and cools, different kinds of heat-loving microbes grow in rings, each with its own colour. The cooler the ring, the more orange and brown it tends to be.

myth: Hot springs are always safe to swim in because the water is natural.

Some hot springs are hot enough to scald badly, and some contain harmful microbes or acids. That is why parks like Yellowstone have boardwalks and strict rules, and why people only bathe in springs that are known to be safe.

sec.t:
A geyser needs three things: plenty of water, a strong source of heat and a narrow, twisting pipe in the rock. Water collects in the pipe and is heated from below. The weight of the water above squeezes it, so it can get hotter than 100 °C without boiling, much like water in a [[@pressure-cooker|pressure cooker]].

Eventually some of it does turn to steam. The steam pushes water out of the top, which lowers the pressure below, so a lot of very hot water suddenly flashes into steam at once. Whoosh. The geyser erupts, then slowly refills and starts again. Yellowstone's [[@old-faithful|Old Faithful]] does this every hour or two.

The name comes from Geysir, a spring in Iceland that once shot water high into the air.

{{story:iceland}}

Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone is more than 100 m across, about as wide as a football field is long. Its centre is deep blue, ringed by yellow, orange and brown.

The colours come from [[microbe|microbes]], living things too small to see. Different kinds survive at different temperatures, so they grow in rings as the water cools on its way out.

In the 1960s, the scientist Thomas Brock found a microbe called Thermus aquaticus living in a Yellowstone spring. It makes chemicals that keep working even when very hot. One of them later became the key ingredient in PCR, a method for copying DNA. PCR is used in crime labs, medical tests and the COVID-19 tests millions of people took. Some of the most [[@microbes-friendly|useful microbes]] live in the strangest places.

India has hundreds of hot springs. At Manikaran, in the Parvati valley of [[@himachal|Himachal Pradesh]], the spring water is very hot. A gurdwara there uses it to cook food for its [[@amritsar|free kitchen]], and Hindu temples stand close by. Further up the valley is Kheerganga, where trekkers soak in a hot pool high in the mountains.

[[@bihar-history|Rajgir in Bihar]] has hot springs mentioned in old Buddhist and Jain stories. In [[@sikkim|Sikkim]], the springs of Yumthang are popular with visitors after a cold drive into the mountains. Many Indian springs smell of rotten eggs, from a gas called hydrogen sulphide that the water carries up from below.

Hot underground water is a source of [[geothermal|geothermal]] energy. In Iceland, it heats most homes. Steam from hot rocks also spins [[turbine|turbines]] to make electricity in places like California, Kenya and [[@new-zealand|New Zealand]]. India has tested geothermal power at sites such as Puga in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]].

Animals enjoy it too. In the mountains of Japan, wild snow monkeys climb into hot springs in winter to warm up.

text: The [[asteroid|asteroid]] was about 10 km wide, tall as a mountain, but tiny compared with Earth.
It was moving about 20 km every second. At that speed you'd go from Mumbai to Pune in 6 seconds.

It made the Chicxulub [[crater|crater]] (say: CHEEK-shoo-loob), about 180 km wide, now buried under Mexico. The impact, about 66 million years ago, set off a chain of disasters that wiped out roughly three-quarters of all kinds of plants and animals, including most dinosaurs.

sec.t:
Ten kilometres is about the height at which passenger jets cruise. Stood on end, the asteroid would have been a little taller than Mount Everest. Earth, by comparison, is almost 12,800 km wide.

What made the asteroid so destructive was its speed. Something moving at 20 km a second carries a staggering amount of energy. When it hit, it punched through the shallow sea and deep into the rock below in a fraction of a second. The rock itself flowed like liquid for a few minutes, then froze into a crater with a ring of peaks inside it, like the splash of a stone in mud.

Scientists think the asteroid was a carbon-rich type. A study published in 2024 suggested that it came from the outer [[solar-system|solar system]], beyond Jupiter, before something knocked it inwards.

Within minutes, a blast of heat and a shower of hot debris spread out from the crater. Giant waves, far bigger than any modern [[tsunami|tsunami]], raced across the young Gulf of Mexico. Rock vapour shot high above the [[atmosphere|atmosphere]], then rained back down across the planet as tiny glassy beads.

The worst effects came later. The impact threw vast amounts of dust, soot and sulphur into the upper air. They spread around the world and blocked much of the sunlight, perhaps for years. Plants and tiny ocean [[organism|organisms]] that need light died off, and the animals that fed on them followed.

{{story:birds-dinosaurs}}

Some animals survived, mostly small ones that could hide, burrow or eat seeds and scraps. Among them were mammals and a few groups of [[@birds-dinosaurs|birds]].

In 1980, the father-and-son scientists Luis and Walter Alvarez studied a thin layer of clay in rocks near Gubbio, in Italy. The clay was full of [[iridium|iridium]], a metal that is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids. They found the same layer around the world, and suggested that a huge asteroid had hit. You can follow that detective story in [[@iridium-evidence|the iridium evidence]].

But where was the crater? In 1978, two geophysicists working for Mexico's state oil company, Glen Penfield and Antonio Camargo, had noticed a giant buried ring under the Yucatán Peninsula while searching for oil. In 1991, Alan Hildebrand and his colleagues showed that this ring was an impact crater of exactly the right age.

Today you can't see Chicxulub from the ground. It lies under about a kilometre of younger rock, half beneath land and half beneath the sea, near the small town of Chicxulub Puerto. The only clue on the surface is a curved line of [[@sinkholes|sinkholes]], called cenotes, that roughly traces the crater's edge.

In 2016, scientists drilled into the crater's ring of peaks from a platform at sea. The rock cores they brought up showed how the crater formed, and how quickly life returned to the area afterwards: within a few years, tiny living things were back.

text: A constellation is a group of stars that people have joined into a picture, and the patch of sky around that picture. Orion the hunter, Scorpius the scorpion and Leo the lion are famous examples.

Long ago, people all over the world grouped the stars into shapes to help them remember the sky, tell stories and keep track of the [[@seasons-why|seasons]]. Today [[astronomer|astronomers]] use 88 official constellations. They divide up the whole sky the way states divide up a country, so any star or [[galaxy|galaxy]] can be given an address, such as "in the constellation Andromeda".

st.prompt: How many official constellations cover the whole sky?
st.reveal: In 1922 the International Astronomical Union agreed on 88 constellations, and a few years later drew exact borders between them. Together they cover every part of the sky, like states on a map.

Then ask a friend to do the same with the same grains. You will probably see completely different pictures, just as different cultures did.
myth: The stars in a constellation are close together in space.
They only look close because they lie in roughly the same direction from Earth. One star in a pattern can be many times farther away than its neighbour.

sec.t:
The stars in a constellation look like they belong together, but that is a trick of [[@perspective|perspective]]. They simply lie in roughly the same direction from Earth.

Take Orion. Its bright stars are scattered at very different distances, some hundreds of [[@light-years|light-years]] farther away than others. If you could fly far across the galaxy and look back, the hunter would fall apart into a jumble of unrelated stars.

It's a bit like standing in a stadium. A player on the field and a fan in the top row might line up perfectly from your seat. From any other seat, they don't.

Every culture has made its own pictures. The bright stars Americans call the Big Dipper are the Plough in Britain and the Saptarishi, or Seven Sages, in India. In many Hindu households the faint star Alcor, beside the middle star of the handle, is linked to Arundhati, the wife of the sage Vasishtha.

Many of the official names come from [[@greek-myths|Greek myths]], passed on through Arabic and Latin books. In the 2nd century CE, the astronomer Ptolemy, working in Alexandria, listed 48 constellations. Most are still in use.

{{story:greek-myths}}

Indian astronomers tracked 27 [[@astronomy-ancient-india|nakshatras]], groups of stars along the path the Moon follows through the sky. The Moon spends roughly one day in each. Nakshatras are still used in [[@indian-calendars|Indian calendars]] to choose dates for festivals and family events.

Ptolemy couldn't see the far southern sky from Alexandria, so his list had a big hole. European sailors heading south in the 1500s noticed unfamiliar stars and began naming them. In the 1750s the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille mapped the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope. He named his new constellations after modern instruments, like the Telescope, the Microscope and the Air Pump.

By the early 1900s, different star maps used different patterns and borders. In 1922 the International Astronomical Union settled on 88 constellations, and its members later drew straight-edged borders between them. The biggest is Hydra, a long water snake. The smallest is Crux, the Southern Cross, which appears on the flags of Australia and New Zealand.

Stars are moving through space at great speed, but they are so far away that their positions barely change in a human lifetime. Over tens of thousands of years, though, the patterns slowly drift. The Big Dipper of 50,000 years from now will look noticeably bent out of shape.

So the constellations we know are a snapshot. People in the future will need new stories for new shapes, and if they live in another part of the galaxy, a completely new sky.

text: On Mars, the colours of the sky are roughly the reverse of ours. In the daytime the sky is a dusty pinkish-orange, often described as butterscotch. At sunset, a cool blue glow spreads around the Sun.

The reason is dust. Mars has a thin [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] that is full of very fine reddish dust, finer than flour. Those dust grains scatter sunlight differently from the gas [[molecule|molecules]] in Earth's air. NASA [[rover|rovers]] have photographed blue Martian sunsets many times.

st.prompt: What colour do you think a Mars sunset is?
st.reveal: Blue! Mars's daytime sky is a dusty butterscotch-pink, but around the setting Sun the fine dust lets blue light through best. NASA rovers have photographed it.
st.nudge: Makes sense for the red planet! But Mars's dust does something surprising.

sec.t:
Mars's air is about one hundredth as thick as ours, so its gas scatters very little light. The dust does the work instead. The grains are much bigger than gas molecules. Their iron-rich colour soaks up some of the blue, and they scatter reddish light widely across the sky. So in daytime the whole sky takes on the dust's warm colour.

Blue light behaves differently with grains that size. More of it carries on almost straight ahead, in the direction the sunlight was already travelling. So the sky right around the Sun looks blue. At sunset, when the light passes through the most dust, that blue halo shows up best.

In April 2015, the Curiosity rover filmed one of these sunsets from Gale Crater. The Sun looked small and pale, wrapped in a soft blue glow.

When NASA's Viking lander sent back the first colour pictures from the surface of Mars in 1976, the first versions showed a blue sky like Earth's. Scientists soon realised the colours had not been balanced properly. Once they corrected them, the sky turned pinkish-tan. Getting colour right from a camera millions of kilometres away is harder than it sounds.

Mars is nicknamed the red planet because its dust and rocks are rich in iron oxide, the same chemical as [[@rust|rust]] on an old bicycle. Winds lift that dust high into the air, so the planet's colour fills its sky too.

Sometimes the dust gets out of hand. In 2018, a storm grew until it covered the whole planet and blocked so much sunlight that the solar-powered Opportunity rover shut down for good.

From Mars, the Sun looks about two-thirds as wide as it does from Earth, because Mars is farther away. Two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, cross the sky. Phobos zips across so quickly that it rises in the west and sets in the east, twice a day.

And Earth? From the Martian surface, our whole planet looks like a bright evening or morning star. Curiosity has photographed it, a small dot of light hanging in the Martian sky.

Mars has clouds too, thin wisps made of water ice, and high up, even of frozen [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. Rovers have photographed them drifting overhead. Some shimmer with pale rainbow colours just after sunset, like mother-of-pearl.

text: Black kites rule [[@urban-wildlife|India's city skies]] because cities give them almost everything they need. Markets, slaughterhouses and rubbish heaps provide food. Tall trees and buildings give them nesting spots. Hot roofs and roads create rising air to soar on.

They are also bold, clever and quick. A black kite can swoop down and snatch a snack from a person's hand, then eat it in mid-air. In [[@hindi-language|Hindi]] it is called the *cheel*. In many Indian cities, from Delhi to Kolkata, it is the large brown bird you see circling high overhead almost every day.

Black kites thrive in crowded cities. They feed on scraps and small animals around markets, rubbish heaps and rivers, and nest in city trees and on buildings.

sec.t:
A black kite has long wings, about 1.5 m from tip to tip, and a forked tail. Watch one closely and you'll see the tail twist and tilt like a rudder as it steers.

On sunny days, roads and roofs heat up and warm air rises from them in invisible columns called thermals. Kites circle inside them and rise for free, without flapping. Then they glide off, scanning the ground with sharp eyes. Some soar high above Delhi for hours. They lose height so slowly that they seem to hang on the wind, which is how the paper [[@kite-flying|kite]] got its English name.

Scientists from the Wildlife Institute of India and the University of Oxford have studied Delhi's kites for years. They found that the city has one of the highest [[density|densities]] of birds of prey anywhere in the world.

Part of the reason is people. In old parts of [[@delhi|Delhi]], many people, especially Muslim families, throw scraps of meat into the air for the kites. For some, it is a religious act of charity, believed to bring blessings or ward off troubles. The kites have learned exactly when and where this happens. This old tradition has quietly helped thousands of birds live in the middle of a huge city.

Not every kite you see in winter is a local. Each year, a larger kind, the black-eared kite, flies in from Central Asia and joins the city birds. In spring, it returns north to breed. So the same tree in Delhi may host local nesters in summer and migrant guests in winter.

{{story:wind-blows}}

Kites have one big human-made danger: kite string. During festivals such as Makar Sankranti and on Independence Day, the sky fills with paper kites. Some strings, called *[[@pop-kites-patang|manja]]*, are coated with powdered glass so they can cut other kites' strings in fights.

Every year, many black kites, pigeons and other birds get tangled in these strings and badly cut. In 2017, India's National Green Tribunal banned glass-coated and synthetic manja across the country, though some is still sold. Volunteers at bird hospitals treat injured birds after every big kite-flying day. The film *All That Breathes*, about two brothers in Delhi who rescue injured kites, was nominated for an Oscar in 2023.

Black kites live across Asia, Africa, Europe and Australia, which makes them one of the most widespread birds of prey on Earth. In northern Australia, Aboriginal people have long told of kites and other hawks picking up burning sticks and dropping them to spread bushfires. The fire drives out small animals, which the birds then catch.

In 2017, scientists published reports from rangers and others who had seen this happen. It is one of very few cases of a wild animal using fire on purpose. City or bush, the black kite is very good at making the most of whatever people, or nature, throw its way. Its big scavenging neighbours, the [[@vultures-india|vultures]], have not been so lucky. And on festival days, the kites share the sky with thousands of paper rivals, as you can read in [[@kites-festival|why India flies kites at Makar Sankranti]].

text: ఆక్టోపస్ చర్మం నిండా వేల కొద్దీ చిన్న చిన్న, సాగే రంగు సంచులు ఉంటాయి. వాటిని క్రోమటోఫోర్లు అంటారు. ఒక్కో సంచి చుట్టూ చిన్న [[@muscles|కండరాలు]] ఉంటాయి. అవి నేరుగా మెదడుకు కలిసి ఉంటాయి. కండరాలు లాగితే సంచి వెడల్పుగా సాగి, దాని రంగు బయటపడుతుంది. వదిలేస్తే అది ముడుచుకుని ఒక చుక్కలా మారుతుంది. ఇదంతా ఒక్క క్షణం కంటే తక్కువ సమయంలో జరిగిపోవచ్చు.

రంగు సంచుల కింద కాంతిని పరావర్తనం చేసే కణాల పొరలు ఉంటాయి. అవి మెరిసే నీలం, ఆకుపచ్చ రంగులను, లేదా సాదా తెలుపును సృష్టిస్తాయి. చర్మం మీద బొడిపెలు, ముళ్లు కూడా లేపగలదు. దాంతో నున్నగా ఉన్న ఆక్టోపస్ ఉన్నట్టుండి గరుకు రాయిలానో నాచు ముద్దలానో మారిపోతుంది.
దాక్కోవడానికి, వేటాడటానికి, సంకేతాలు పంపడానికి ఆక్టోపస్‌లు ఈ ఉపాయాలను వాడతాయి. ఇలా మారువేషం వేయడాన్ని [[@camouflage|కామఫ్లాజ్]] అంటారు.

sec.t:
ఇక్కడే విచిత్రం ఉంది. చాలా ఆక్టోపస్‌లకు రంగులు కనిపించవు. వాటి కళ్లలో కాంతిని గుర్తించే కణాలు ఒకే రకం ఉంటాయి. కాబట్టి అవి ప్రపంచాన్ని ఒకే రంగు ఛాయల్లో చూస్తాయి అనిపిస్తుంది. అయినా చుట్టూ ఉన్న రంగులను అవి చక్కగా అనుకరిస్తాయి.

అది ఎలాగో ఎవరికీ సరిగ్గా తెలియదు. ఒక ఆధారం ఏమిటంటే, కళ్లలో కాంతిని గుర్తించే [[protein|ప్రొటీన్లే]] ఆక్టోపస్ చర్మంలోనూ ఉన్నాయి. 2015లో జరిగిన ఒక అధ్యయనంలో, కాలిఫోర్నియా ఆక్టోపస్ చర్మం ముక్కలు మెదడు నుంచి వేరు చేసిన తర్వాత కూడా కాంతికి స్పందించాయి. ఇంకో ఆలోచన ఏంటంటే, వాటి వింత ఆకారపు [[pupil|కనుపాపలు]] రంగులను వేరు చేసి చూడటానికి సాయపడవచ్చు. ఈ రెండు ఆలోచనలనూ ఇంకా పరీక్షిస్తున్నారు.

2016లో న్యూజిలాండ్ నేషనల్ అక్వేరియంలో ఇంకీ అనే ఆక్టోపస్ తన తొట్టి నుంచి జారుకుంది. నేల మీద పాకుతూ వెళ్లి, ఒక డ్రైనేజీ పైపులోకి దూరి, తిరిగి సముద్రం చేరుకుంది. సిబ్బందికి తడి గుర్తుల దారి తప్ప ఇంకేమీ దొరకలేదు.

లోపల ఉన్న తిండి కోసం ఆక్టోపస్‌లు సీసా మూతలను తిప్పి తీయగలవు. ఇండోనేషియాలో నరాల ఆక్టోపస్‌లు (వెయిన్డ్ ఆక్టోపస్‌లు) సగం కొబ్బరి చిప్పలను మోసుకుంటూ తిరిగి, వాటిలో దాక్కోవడం వీడియోలో రికార్డయింది. [[@crow-smart|తెలివైన కాకుల]] లాగా, ఇలా పనిముట్లు వాడటం క్షీరదాలు, పక్షులు తప్ప ఇతర జంతువుల్లో అరుదు అని ఒకప్పుడు అనుకునేవాళ్లు. [[@seattle|సియాటిల్‌లోని]] ఒక అక్వేరియంలో, పెద్ద పసిఫిక్ ఆక్టోపస్‌లు ఒకే యూనిఫాం వేసుకున్న ఇద్దరు సంరక్షకులను వేరు వేరుగా గుర్తుపట్టడం నేర్చుకున్నాయి. ఒకరు వాటికి తిండి పెట్టేవారు. ఇంకొకరు ముళ్ల కర్రతో మెల్లగా పొడిచేవారు. 2010లో జర్మనీ అక్వేరియంలోని పాల్ అనే ఆక్టోపస్ రెండు తిండి డబ్బాల్లో ఒకదాన్ని ఎంచుకుంటూ, [[@fifa-world-cup|ఫుట్‌బాల్ ప్రపంచకప్]] మ్యాచుల్లో గెలిచేవాళ్లను ‘ముందే చెప్పింది’.

ఇంత తెలివి ఉన్నా, చాలా ఆక్టోపస్‌లు ఒకటి రెండు ఏళ్లే బతుకుతాయి. తల్లి ఆక్టోపస్ ఒక గుహలో గుడ్లు పెట్టి వాటికి కాపలా కాస్తుంది. వాటిని శుభ్రం చేస్తూ, వాటి మీదకు తాజా నీళ్లు ఊదుతూ ఉంటుంది. సాధారణంగా ఆ సమయంలో తిండి మానేస్తుంది. పిల్లలు బయటికి వచ్చిన కొద్ది రోజులకే చనిపోతుంది.

కాలిఫోర్నియా తీరంలో లోతైన సముద్రంలోని ఒక ఆక్టోపస్ తన గుడ్లను సుమారు నాలుగున్నర ఏళ్లు కాపాడింది. తెలిసిన జంతువులన్నిటిలో అదే అతి ఎక్కువ కాలం. అంతకు ముందే ప్రమాదం ముంచుకొస్తే, ఆక్టోపస్‌ల దగ్గర ఇంకో ఉపాయం ఉంది. తప్పించుకోవడానికి వీలుగా [[@octopus-ink|సిరా]] మేఘాన్ని చిమ్ముతాయి. వాటి బంధువులైన కటిల్‌ఫిష్, స్క్విడ్‌లు కూడా రంగులు మార్చగలవు. [[@coral-reefs|పగడపు దిబ్బ]] మీద ఈ మూడూ వెలుగుల ప్రదర్శన చేస్తాయి. ఆ భాషను చదవడం శాస్త్రవేత్తలు ఇంకా నేర్చుకుంటూనే ఉన్నారు.

2022లో యునైటెడ్ కింగ్‌డమ్ తన జంతు సంక్షేమ చట్టాన్ని మార్చి, అందులో ఆక్టోపస్‌లు, స్క్విడ్‌లు, కటిల్‌ఫిష్‌లను కూడా చేర్చింది. వాటికి [[@pain|నొప్పి]] తెలుస్తుందనడానికి బలమైన ఆధారాలు ఉన్నాయని ఒక శాస్త్రీయ సమీక్షలో తేలిన తర్వాత ఈ మార్పు వచ్చింది. ఇలా చేసిన మొదటి దేశాల్లో అది ఒకటి.

text: Naked mole rats are wrinkly, pink, almost hairless rodents that live underground in East Africa. They are about the size of a mouse. A mouse might live two to four years. A naked mole rat can live for more than 30.

Even more surprising, cancer is extremely rare in them. Scientists have found several reasons. Their cells make a thick, gooey substance that seems to stop them clumping into tumours. Their cells are also very quick to stop dividing when they get crowded. And their bodies seem extra good at fixing damaged [[protein|proteins]].
They are not completely cancer-proof. But they are so good at avoiding it that labs around the world study them.

sec.t:
Your body is made of trillions of [[@body-cells|cells]], and most of them copy themselves now and then. Cancer starts when some cells keep copying when they shouldn't, piling up into a lump.

In 2013, scientists at the University of Rochester in New York found something odd. Naked mole rat cells were making huge amounts of a substance called hyaluronan. This is a sugary material found in many animals, including us, in joints and skin. But the mole rat version was about five times bigger, with extra-long [[molecule|molecules]].

It made their cells very sensitive to crowding. As soon as cells touched each other, they stopped dividing. When the researchers removed this thick hyaluronan, the cells became much more likely to turn cancerous.

Most animals get weaker and more likely to die as they get older. Naked mole rats seem to break this rule. In 2018, scientists studied records from thousands of animals and found that their risk of dying barely rose with age, even after 25 years.

That makes them strange champions of [[@ageing|ageing]]. Old mole rats still breed, stay strong and keep their bones healthy. Scientists hope that learning their secrets might one day help people stay healthier for longer, although that is a long way off.

Naked mole rats live in big underground colonies, digging tunnels with their long front teeth. Their lips close behind their teeth, so they can dig without swallowing soil.

Like [[@bees-dance|bees]] and ants, they live in a colony with one breeding queen. A few males breed with her. Everyone else works: digging, finding roots to eat, guarding against snakes or caring for pups. A colony can hold up to about 300 animals. They even share a toilet chamber, and when one fills up, they seal it off and dig a new one.

Their burrows have very little oxygen. In 2017, scientists found that naked mole rats survived 18 minutes with no oxygen at all. Their bodies switched to burning fructose, a sugar found in fruit, which needs no oxygen to release energy. They also feel very little pain from some [[acid|acids]] that would hurt other animals.

{{story:extreme-longest-living}}

sec.h: Each colony has its own accent
sec.t:
Naked mole rats chirp to each other all the time. In 2021, scientists recorded thousands of soft chirps from different colonies. They found that each colony had its own [[dialect|dialect]], a slightly different way of chirping.

Mole rats answered more often to the chirps of their own colony. When pups were raised in a different colony, they learned that colony's dialect. The queen may help keep the dialect steady.

This is one of the clearest examples of a "culture" of calls in rodents, a topic explored in [[@animal-communication|animal communication]]. And the strangest part? These wrinkly diggers live in the same dry lands of [[@kenya-safari|Kenya]] where elephants and lions roam above them, completely unaware of the busy cities under their feet.

text: Big countries like India and the USA are [[federal|federal]], which means power is shared between a national government and state governments. Each state has its own government with its own leader, lawmakers and civil servants.

State governments run much of what touches daily life: police, hospitals, most schools, state roads, farming support, water and land records. In India, the state's elected head is the Chief Minister, who leads a council of ministers. The Governor, appointed by the President, is the formal head of the state. In the USA, each state elects its own governor, who is the real head of the state government, a bit like a president for that state.

sec.t:
India's Constitution lists who controls what in three lists. The Union List, for the central government, includes defence, railways, foreign affairs and [[currency|currency]]. The State List includes police, public health, agriculture, prisons and local government. The Concurrent List, shared by both, includes education, forests and marriage laws. If the two clash on a shared subject, the central law usually wins.

States pass some of their own work further down. Since 1992, the Constitution has required states to hand certain powers and funds to elected [[@panchayat|panchayats]] in villages and to municipalities in towns. How much they actually hand over varies a lot from state to state.

India has 28 states and 8 union [[territory|territories]]. Union territories are run more directly by the central government, though Delhi, [[@puducherry|Puducherry]], and Jammu and Kashmir have their own elected assemblies.

{{story:states-india}}

Every Indian state has a legislative assembly, or Vidhan Sabha, elected every five years. The party or alliance with a majority chooses the Chief Minister. Six states, including Maharashtra, Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh, also have an upper house, the Legislative Council.

The Governor's job is mostly formal, but it matters at certain moments. When no party has a clear majority, the Governor invites someone to try to form a government. If a state's government breaks down, the President can impose President's Rule, and the state is run from Delhi for a time. Governors and elected state governments sometimes clash, and some of these disputes have reached the Supreme Court.

In the USA, [[@usa-statehood|the original 13 states]] existed before the national government, and all [[@states-usa|50 states]] keep wide powers. Each has its own [[constitution|constitution]], its own courts and its own laws on things like driving ages, school rules and criminal punishments.

Every state elects a governor, usually for four years. The governor proposes the state budget, signs or [[veto|vetoes]] bills, commands the state's National Guard and can pardon prisoners. Every state except Nebraska has a two-house legislature. Nebraska's single house, set up in 1937, is also officially non-partisan, so members don't run under party labels.

States let a huge country be run closer to the people. India redrew many of its state borders by language in 1956, so that people could deal with government in their own language, like Tamil, Telugu or [[@marathi-gujarati|Marathi]]. That is one reason [[@languages-india|India's languages]] remain so strong.

States also try new ideas. In the USA, some states let women vote decades before the whole country did. Tamil Nadu's school lunch programme helped inspire India's national [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meal]] scheme. When one state tries something that works, others often copy it.

text: People shake hands to greet, to agree and to show trust. A handshake says "we are equals" and "I mean you no harm". It is used to meet new people, finish a deal, congratulate a winner or make peace after an argument.

Nobody knows exactly where it started. Pictures of handshakes go back nearly 3,000 years, to ancient Assyria in today's Iraq. Ancient Greeks carved them on gravestones. A popular story says people offered an open right hand to show they had no weapon, and shaking it up and down would shake loose any hidden dagger. That is a nice tale, but there is no strong evidence for it.

st.reveal: Researchers in Wales dipped gloved hands in bacteria and tested greetings. A handshake passed on about ten times as many bacteria as a fist bump. A high five was in between. Shorter contact and less touching skin meant fewer germs.

sec.t:
On a carved throne base from about 850 BCE, the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III is shown clasping hands with a Babylonian king to seal an alliance. It is one of the oldest known images of a handshake. In [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], the gesture meant a deal was agreed.

In [[@ancient-greece|ancient Greece]], from the 5th century BCE, gravestones often show the dead person shaking hands with a family member. It may have meant a farewell, or the bond between them continuing after death. Greeks called this gesture *dexiosis*, the joining of right hands. The Romans used handshakes for promises and marriages.

The handshake is not used everywhere. In India, many people greet with *namaste*, pressing palms together, sometimes with a small bow. It needs no touch, and it is a sign of respect. In Japan, people bow, and the depth of the bow shows how much respect is meant.

In France and parts of South America, friends often kiss on the cheek. Maori people in New Zealand perform the *hongi*, pressing noses and foreheads together. In some cultures, men and women who are not related don't touch at all when greeting. Knowing what to do takes practice, and getting it wrong can be awkward.

Hands carry germs. That's why [[@body-handwashing-history|washing hands]] is one of the best ways to stop illness spreading. In 2014, researchers in Wales tested greetings with gloves dipped in [[bacteria|bacteria]]. A handshake passed on many more bacteria than a high five, and about ten times as many as a fist bump.

When COVID-19 spread in 2020, handshakes almost vanished. People tried elbow bumps, foot taps, waves and namaste. World leaders were seen greeting each other with folded hands. Many people predicted handshakes would never return. In most places, though, they came back.

Many people believe a handshake reveals something about a person. A firm grip is often seen as confident. A limp one can seem shy or unfriendly. Some studies suggest people do judge each other on handshakes, though first impressions can be wrong.

In sport, handshakes mark respect. Cricketers shake hands after a match. Footballers shake hands before kick-off. In business, a handshake has long sealed a deal, even before the contract is signed. It is a tiny gesture with a long history, and it stays alive because humans everywhere want a way to show trust. How the rest of the world says hello is a story told in [[@life-greetings|greetings]] from Tokyo to Timbuktu.

text: Life in the Indian Army is a mix of hard training, strict routine, long postings far from home and a very close bond with the people you serve beside. A soldier might spend two or three years at a base in the plains, then be sent to guard a snowy border post or a forest in the Northeast.

The Indian Army is one of the largest in the world, with about 12 lakh active soldiers. They come from every state and many languages. Most of their time is spent not fighting but training, guarding India's long borders and helping during disasters.

st.reveal: Helicopters help, but they cannot fly in every kind of weather. Thousands of army mules still carry food, fuel and ammunition up narrow mountain tracks, and soldiers carry loads where even mules cannot go.

sec.t:
At most army bases, the day starts before sunrise with a bugle call called reveille. Then comes physical training: running, push-ups, rope climbing and drills. After breakfast, soldiers practise their skills, look after their weapons and vehicles, and study.

Meals are eaten together in a mess or a langar. Evenings often include games of volleyball or football. Army life runs on timetables, uniforms and orders, and discipline matters because in a crisis everyone must know exactly what to do.

Officers usually train at the National Defence Academy near Pune, joining at around 16 to 19, then at the Indian Military Academy in Dehradun. Since 2022, girls can join the National Defence Academy too.

sec.h: Living on the edge of the map
sec.t:
Some postings are among the toughest anywhere. On the Siachen Glacier in the Karakoram, Indian posts sit above 6,000 metres. At that [[@altitude|altitude]], each breath holds about half the oxygen it would at sea level. Temperatures can drop to around minus 50°C, and storms can last for days.

Soldiers there wear layers of special clothing, live in insulated huts and must be swapped out after a few months, because the body cannot cope for long. Supplies come by helicopter, or on foot and by [[@donkeys-mules|mule]] along icy tracks.

Other soldiers guard hot deserts in Rajasthan, where summer days pass 45°C, or the thick forests of the Northeast.

Army families move often, every two or three years. Children may go to a new school each time, often a Kendriya Vidyalaya or Army Public School, where most classmates are also army kids. Many say they grew up with friends in every corner of India.

Bases, called cantonments, have their own shops, hospitals and parks. When a parent is posted to a remote border, the family usually stays behind, and phone calls may be rare.

Since 2022, many young people join through a scheme called Agnipath, serving for four years. A share of them are then chosen to stay on for a full career. Women have served as army officers for decades and, since a 2020 Supreme Court ruling, can serve full careers as officers too.

When floods, earthquakes or landslides strike, the army is often among the first to arrive. Its engineers build temporary bridges, its doctors run field hospitals and its trucks carry food. In 2024, after deadly landslides in Wayanad, Kerala, army engineers built a 190-foot steel bridge in about 31 hours so rescuers could reach cut-off villages.

Indian soldiers also serve abroad as UN [[@peacekeepers|peacekeepers]]. India has been one of the biggest contributors of troops to UN missions for decades. And every year on 26 January, soldiers from many regiments march down Kartavya Path in Delhi in the [[@republic-day-parade|Republic Day parade]], each regiment in its own colours.

text: The metre was invented in France in the 1790s. Scientists wanted a unit that belonged to nobody, not to any king or town, and would never change. So they based it on the Earth itself.

They decided a metre would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the [[equator|equator]], measured along the line of longitude that runs through [[@paris|Paris]]. To find that distance, two [[astronomer|astronomers]] spent seven years measuring part of it by hand.
The metre has been redefined several times since, each time more precisely. Today it is fixed using the speed of light.

st.reveal: The metre was meant to be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator. That makes a quarter of the way round the Earth 10,000 km, and the whole way round about 40,000 km. The measurement was slightly off, but very close.

sec.t:
Before the [[@french-revolution|French Revolution of 1789]], France had a mess of measures. One estimate says there were about 250,000 local versions of units in use. A "pound" or a "foot" in one town could be different in the next. Traders cheated, and arguments were endless.

The new revolutionary government wanted fairness and reason. In 1791, the French Academy of Sciences recommended basing a new unit of length on the size of the Earth. It was named the *mètre*, from a Greek word for "measure". Everything else would be built from it in tens. A litre would be [[@area-volume|the volume of a box]] 10 cm on each side. A kilogram would be the mass of a litre of water.

Two astronomers, Jean-Baptiste Delambre and Pierre Méchain, were sent to measure the distance from Dunkirk, on the northern coast of France, to Barcelona in [[@spain|Spain]]. Delambre started in the north, Méchain in the south.

They worked by triangulation. From hilltops and church towers, they measured the angles between distant landmarks to build a long chain of triangles. With careful [[@shapes-angles|geometry]], the angles and one measured base line revealed the full distance.

It was slow and sometimes dangerous. France was at war, and the astronomers were arrested more than once by suspicious locals who thought their instruments were for spying. Méchain later found a small error in his own measurements and kept it secret, which troubled him for the rest of his life.

In 1799, the result was made into a bar of platinum, the "metre of the Archives".

{{story:light-years}}

Other countries were slow to join at first. In 1875, seventeen nations, including the United States, signed the Metre Convention in Paris and set up an international office to look after the units. In 1889, new metal bars of platinum and [[iridium|iridium]] were made and copies sent to each country.

Over the next century, most of the world adopted the system. India's metric law was passed in 1956. Today almost every country uses metric units for science, trade and daily life.

A metal bar has problems. It can be scratched, it grows a tiny bit in heat, and there is only one original. So in 1960, scientists redefined the metre using the light given off by krypton [[atom|atoms]].

In 1983, they went further. Light in a [[vacuum|vacuum]] always travels at the same speed, so they fixed that speed at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second. A metre became the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second. That is the same idea astronomers use when they measure space in [[@light-years|light-years]].

In 2019, the kilogram was also redefined using a constant of nature, so the last metal standard was retired. The [[@gps-how|GPS]] in your phone depends on [[@time-measure|measuring time]] and distance with this kind of accuracy.

text: The Pythagorean theorem is a rule about right-angled triangles, the kind with one square corner. If you build a square on each of the three sides, the two smaller squares together have exactly the same area as the biggest one. In symbols, a² + b² = c², where c is the longest side, called the hypotenuse.

The classic example is a triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5. 3 × 3 is 9, and 4 × 4 is 16. Together that makes 25, which is 5 × 5. The rule works for every right-angled triangle, large or small, and it lets you find a missing side whenever you know the other two.

st.reveal: Screens are measured on the diagonal, which is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle. A screen 40 inches wide and 30 inches high has a diagonal of 50 inches, because 40² + 30² = 1,600 + 900 = 2,500, and 50² = 2,500.

sec.t:
Pythagoras was a Greek thinker born on the island of Samos around 570 BCE. He later settled in southern Italy, where he led a group of followers who studied numbers, music and the stars. They believed numbers were the key to understanding the universe.

We know surprisingly little about him for certain. He wrote nothing that survives, and many stories about him were written centuries after he died. His followers often credited their own discoveries to their famous teacher. So the theorem carries his name, but nobody can be sure he proved it himself.

Because the theorem is so simple and so useful, people have kept finding new ways to prove it. An American teacher named Elisha Loomis collected them in a book. Its first edition came out in 1927, and the 1940 edition contained 367 proofs.

One of them came from James Garfield. In 1876, while he was a member of the [[@congress-usa|US Congress]], Garfield worked out a proof using a trapezium made of three triangles. It was published in a journal for teachers. The journal's note said he found it during friendly maths discussions with other members of Congress. After more than 2,000 years, the theorem was still a puzzle worth playing with. Five years later, he became the 20th President of the United States.

The theorem turns up everywhere. Builders use the 3-4-5 rule to check that the corners of a room are square. Firefighters use it to work out how long a ladder must be to reach a window. A ladder leaning against a wall, the ground and the wall make a right-angled triangle.

Screens are measured using it too. The size of a TV or a [[@smartphones|smartphone]] screen is the length of its diagonal. Computers use the theorem constantly to find the distance between two points. A video game uses it to tell how far your character is from a monster. A delivery app uses it to estimate how far a rider is from your door. A rule from clay tablets now runs inside almost every device you own.

text: LEGO began in 1932 in Billund, a village in Denmark, when a carpenter named Ole Kirk Christiansen started making wooden toys. In 1934 he named his company LEGO, from the Danish words "leg godt", meaning "play well".

In 1949 the company began making plastic building bricks, based on [[@pop-lego-history|a British design]]. In 1958 it patented a new brick with tubes inside that made models hold together firmly. That design has barely changed since, which is why bricks from the 1950s still fit with ones made today.

st.reveal: The 1958 design added hollow tubes inside each brick. The studs of the brick below press between the tubes and the walls, which grips them tightly. Engineers call this clutch power.

myth: LEGO was named after a Latin word meaning "I put together".
The name comes from the Danish "leg godt", meaning "play well". The company later noticed that "lego" in Latin can mean "I gather" or "I put together", but that was a happy coincidence.

sec.t:
Christiansen was a carpenter who made furniture and houses. In the early 1930s, during a worldwide economic slump, farmers could no longer afford new buildings. To keep his workshop going, he began making wooden toys, including [[@yo-yo-tops|yo-yos]], trucks and pull-along ducks.

His motto was "only the best is good enough". A famous family story says his son once saved money by using only two coats of varnish on some toy ducks instead of three. Christiansen sent him back to the railway station to fetch them and finish the job.

In 1958 Ole Kirk's son Godtfred Kirk Christiansen and his team found the solution: hollow tubes inside the brick. The studs of one brick press between the tubes and walls of the brick above, gripping firmly. The patent was filed on 28 January 1958, and the design is still the basis of LEGO bricks.

Soon after, a fire destroyed the company's wooden toy warehouse. LEGO decided to concentrate on plastic bricks, and by 1960 it had stopped making wooden toys.

sec.h: Built to a fraction of a hair
sec.t:
Since 1963, LEGO bricks have been made from a tough plastic called ABS. The moulds are made so accurately that the bricks differ by only a few thousandths of a millimetre, much less than the width of a human hair. That precision is why billions of bricks, made in different factories and decades apart, all fit together.

In 2005 the Danish mathematician Søren Eilers used a computer to count how many ways six 2×4 bricks can be joined. The answer, 915,103,765, shows how fast possibilities grow, an example of [[@big-numbers|big numbers]] hiding in a toy box.

The smiling minifigure arrived in 1978. Themed sets based on space, [[@knights-castles|castles]] and later films followed. The first LEGOLAND park opened in Billund in 1968.

Around 2003 the company nearly went bankrupt after expanding too fast into other products. It recovered by focusing on its bricks again. Today LEGO kits are used in schools to teach [[@programming|coding]] and [[@robots|robots]], and in competitions where teams build machines.

LEGO is trying to make bricks from recycled or plant-based plastic, but it has proved hard to match the strength of ABS. Old bricks rarely end up in the bin. They are handed down to younger cousins and siblings, which makes LEGO one of the most passed-on [[@toys-history|toys]] in history, and slows the need for [[@recycling|recycling]].

text: Music streaming means playing songs over the internet instead of from a file you own. The songs are kept on huge computers, called [[server|servers]], in [[@data-centres|data centres]] around the world. When you press play, the server sends the song to your phone in small chunks, and your phone plays each chunk as it arrives.

To make this fast, songs are squeezed into small files. A three-minute song at normal quality is about 3 megabytes, small enough to start almost instantly on a mobile network. Apps such as Spotify, JioSaavn, Gaana and YouTube Music hold around 100 million songs this way.

st.prompt: A song plays smoothly even when your internet slows down for a moment. Why?

options.t: Your phone keeps the next few seconds ready in a buffer
The singer slows down to match your internet
The song is stored inside the phone's speaker

st.reveal: Apps load a little ahead of what you are hearing and keep it in a short-term store called a buffer. If the connection drops briefly, the music plays from the buffer. If the gap lasts longer, the song stops and waits.

d.try: Play a song you know on the lowest and highest quality setting your music app allows, using headphones if you can. Listen carefully to cymbals and the singer's breath. Can you hear a difference, or does your brain fill in the gaps?
myth: When you stream a song, it is stored on your phone forever.
Normally the pieces are kept only briefly and then thrown away. Downloads for offline listening are saved in locked files that usually stop working if you stop paying.

sec.t:
Sound is a wave of vibrating air. A microphone turns that wave into an electrical signal, and a computer measures the signal tens of thousands of times every second. Each measurement is stored as a number, in [[@binary-code|binary code]], the ones and zeros computers use.

CD-quality sound takes 44,100 measurements a second for each ear. That makes a lot of numbers: a three-minute song comes to about 30 megabytes. Sending that much data to millions of phones at once would be slow and expensive, so engineers found a way to shrink it.

sec.h: Throwing away what you can't hear

sec.t:
When you tap a song, your app asks a server for it. The song is split into small pieces that travel across the [[@internet-how|internet]], sometimes by different routes, and are put back in order on your phone.

The app always loads a little ahead, keeping a few seconds in a buffer. That's why a song can keep playing through a short tunnel on a train. Popular songs are copied onto servers in many cities, so a listener in Chennai and one in Chicago are each served from somewhere nearby.

sec.h: How apps choose your next song
sec.t:
Streaming apps track what you play, skip, repeat and save. Computer programs, or [[@algorithms|algorithms]], compare your habits with millions of other listeners. If people who like the same songs as you also love a new song, the app may suggest it.

Some services also analyse the sound itself, such as its speed, its instruments and how energetic it is. This is how a playlist can move from one song to a similar one without anyone choosing each track by hand.

Listeners pay a monthly fee, or listen free with adverts. The service keeps part of the money and shares the rest with record companies, songwriters and singers, based roughly on how many times each song is played.

Each play earns only a tiny fraction of a rupee. Many musicians say this is too little unless a song is played millions of times. Streaming services say it brings music to far more people than CDs ever did. The argument is still going on, and the rules keep changing.

text: Yoga and Ayurveda are two old Indian traditions that both grew up around the same ideas: that body and mind are connected, and that health comes from balance.
Ayurveda is a system of medicine. Its name means "knowledge of life" in [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]]. It uses herbs, diet, massage, daily routines and, in its classical form, even surgery.

Yoga is a set of practices for the body and mind: breathing [[@exercise|exercises]], meditation and physical postures. Today it is practised by millions of people around the world, many of whom think of it mainly as exercise.

st.prompt: The word "yoga" comes from Sanskrit. What does its root word mean?
st.reveal: Yoga comes from the root yuj, to join or yoke, the same idea as yoking two oxen to a cart. It is the ancestor of the English word "yoke".

d.try: Stand on one foot with your other foot resting against your ankle or calf, like the tree pose. Ask a friend to time how long you can balance with your eyes open, then with your eyes closed. Most people wobble much sooner with their eyes shut, because your eyes help your inner ear keep you steady.
myth: Yoga is mostly about twisting your body into difficult poses.

In the ancient texts, yoga is mainly about training the mind through breathing, concentration and meditation. The many standing and flowing poses popular today were largely developed in the last 150 years.

sec.h: Three doshas and a cook's spice box

sec.t:
The most famous early yoga text is the *Yoga Sutras* of Patanjali, a collection of short sayings. Scholars disagree on its date, but many place it somewhere between 1,600 and 2,200 years ago.

Patanjali describes eight "limbs" of yoga. They include rules for behaviour, breath control, withdrawing the senses and, finally, deep concentration and meditation. Posture is only one limb, and he says little about it beyond sitting steady and at ease. Breath control matters more, and works because [[@lungs-breathe|your lungs]] and heart rate are closely linked.

Yoga's ideas reached America before its poses did. In 1893, the Indian monk [[@swami-vivekananda|Swami Vivekananda]] spoke at the Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago and became famous overnight. He went on to teach yoga [[philosophy|philosophy]] and meditation in the USA, and in 1896 published a book on it called *Raja Yoga*. For many Americans, it was their first meeting with these ideas.

Modern posture yoga took shape in the early 1900s. In Mysore, a teacher named T. Krishnamacharya developed flowing sequences of poses. His students, including B.K.S. Iyengar and K. Pattabhi Jois, taught them around the world.

In the USA, yoga grew from a curiosity to a common activity. A 2017 US government survey found that about one in seven American adults had practised it in the past year. In 2014, the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] declared 21 June the International Day of Yoga, and the first was held in 2015.

Researchers have studied [[@yoga-science|yoga]] a lot. There is good evidence that it can improve flexibility and balance, and some evidence that it helps with back pain and [[@stress|stress]]. It is not a cure for serious illness.

Ayurveda is harder to test, because treatments are often tailored to each person. Some herbs are being studied seriously. Others have little evidence behind them, and a 2004 study found that about one in five Ayurvedic products bought in Boston shops contained harmful metals such as lead. Ayurveda practitioners say the traditional knowledge has value; many doctors want stronger proof from [[@statistics-lies|careful trials]].

India's government supports both through the Ministry of AYUSH, set up in 2014. Anyone with a real illness should still see a qualified doctor.

text: In a bilingual brain, both languages are always switched on. When you hear or think of a word, matching words in both languages wake up. Your brain then picks the one you need and pushes the other one down, many times a minute, without you noticing.

This constant choosing uses brain areas that also handle attention and self-control. Scientists are studying whether all that practice changes the brain in useful ways. Some think it does. Others say the effects are small or hard to prove.

st.prompt: Does learning two languages at once confuse young children and slow down their speech?

options.t: No, children can learn two languages without harm
Yes, they should learn one language first
Yes, but only if the languages use different scripts

st.reveal: Studies find bilingual children reach the big speech milestones at about the same ages as other children. They may know fewer words in each language at first, but add both together and they usually know as many or more.

src: Ellen Bialystok and colleagues, research on bilingualism and the brain (York University, Canada).
Census of India 2011, language data (Office of the Registrar General, Government of India).
n.certNote: Scientists agree that bilingual brains juggle both languages all the time. Whether this gives lasting benefits, such as sharper attention or later memory loss in old age, is still hotly debated.

d.try: Ask someone who speaks two languages to name as many fruits as they can in one minute in one language, then in the other. Notice whether they mix words, pause or switch. Ask them which language they count in, dream in or use when they're angry.
myth: Learning two languages at once confuses children and delays their speech.
Research shows bilingual children develop language normally. Mixing words from both languages is a normal stage, not a sign of confusion, and many adults do it on purpose too.
facts: Indians who speak two or more languages
Americans who speak a language other than English at home
Babies tune in to their home languages
active in the brain at the same time
Switching between languages in one sentence

sec.t:
You don't have a separate box for each language. Both share the same main language areas, mostly on the left side of the brain. Words from both languages are stored in an overlapping web, linked to the same ideas.

So if a girl in Chennai who speaks Tamil and English sees a dog, both "naai" and "dog" light up. If she's talking to her English teacher, her brain holds back the Tamil word. With her grandmother, it does the opposite. Most of the time she doesn't feel any of this. The choosing happens in a fraction of a second. Brain scans show extra activity in control areas at the front of the brain while this happens.

Newborns can hear the difference between speech sounds from every language. A baby in Kolkata could tell apart sounds used only in Japanese. But by around their first birthday, babies get better at their home languages' sounds and worse at others.

Babies who hear two languages from birth keep both sets of sounds. Their [[@brain-development|brains grow]] networks for each, and they sort the languages out surprisingly early. Some studies suggest they can even tell two languages apart by watching a speaker's face.

Since the 2000s, some studies have suggested bilingual people are better at ignoring distractions and switching between tasks. Others found no such advantage once they compared people of similar backgrounds. Scientists now argue over how big any benefit really is.

There's a similar debate about old age. Dementia is a disease that slowly damages memory. A study in Canada, and a larger one in Hyderabad in 2013, found that bilingual patients showed its first signs about four years later, on average, than people who spoke one language. Some later studies didn't find this. For now, the honest answer is "maybe".

You can become bilingual at any age, though most people who learn after childhood keep an accent. Adults often learn grammar faster than children at first, while children are better at sounding like native speakers in the long run.

India is a good place to try. In the 2011 [[census|census]] about a quarter of Indians said they spoke at least two languages, and many speak three or more. People who use [[@sign-language|sign language]] alongside a spoken language are bilingual too. Most experts on [[@learning-languages|learning languages]] give the same simple tip: use the new language with real people, often, even if you make mistakes. Songs, cartoons and comics help too, because your brain remembers words better when they come with a story or a tune.

text: Your brain is made of about 86 billion nerve cells, called [[neuron|neurons]]. Each one is a long, thin cell with branches that reach out to other neurons. Together they form a web with trillions of connections.

Neurons talk using electricity and chemicals. A tiny electrical signal races along a neuron. When it reaches the end, the neuron squirts out chemicals that cross a gap and switch on the next cell. Every thought, feeling and movement is a pattern of these signals flickering through the web.
Your brain gets information from your senses, compares it with what it has learned, and sends out instructions, all in a fraction of a second.

st.prompt: Your brain is only about 2% of your body weight. Roughly how much of your body's energy does it use?
st.reveal: About a fifth. Your brain never really switches off, even in sleep. Its billions of nerve cells keep firing signals day and night, and that takes a steady supply of sugar and oxygen from your blood.

src: Azevedo F.A.C. et al. (2009) Equal numbers of neuronal and nonneuronal cells make the human brain an isometrically scaled-up primate brain. Journal of Comparative Neurology 513.
US National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, Brain Basics.

d.try: Ask a friend to hold a ruler upright, with the zero end just above your open thumb and finger. Without warning, they let go, and you catch it as fast as you can. The centimetre mark where you caught it shows your reaction time. Try ten catches and see if your brain gets faster with practice.
myth: We only use 10% of our brains.

Brain scans show activity all over the brain, though not every part is busy at once. Even simple jobs like catching a ball use many areas together. Damage to almost any part of the brain affects something.

sec.t:
The biggest part is the *cerebrum*, the wrinkled dome on top. It handles thinking, language, seeing, planning and deciding. Its wrinkles fold a large sheet of brain into a small skull, like scrunching a big dupatta into a small bag.

Tucked underneath at the back is the *cerebellum*. It keeps your balance and smooths your movements, so you can ride a bicycle or bowl a cricket ball without thinking about every muscle.

The *brainstem* joins the brain to the spinal cord. It runs the jobs you never think about, such as breathing, heartbeat and swallowing.

The cerebrum is split into two halves. Oddly, the left half controls the right side of your body, and the right half controls the left. The nerves cross over on their way down.

You may have heard that "left-brained" people are logical and "right-brained" people are creative. Scientists have found no good evidence for this. The two halves do have some special jobs, but they work as a team, linked by a thick bridge of about 20 crore nerve fibres.

Every time you practise something, like a [[@tabla|tabla]] [[rhythm|rhythm]] or a long division sum, connections between certain neurons get stronger. Ones you don't use can weaken. Scientists call this ability to change *plasticity*. It's why practice works, and why children pick up new languages so easily.

[[@computers-how|Computers]] use electricity too, but they work very differently. A laptop does one step after another at enormous speed. Your brain is much slower per step but does billions of things at the same time, using about as much power as a dim light bulb.

sec.h: The man with the iron rod
sec.t: In 1848, a railway worker in Vermont named Phineas Gage survived a terrible accident. An iron rod shot through the front of his head. He recovered and could walk and talk, but people who knew him said his personality changed. Doctors studied him for years. His case helped show that different parts of the brain do different jobs, and that the front of the brain helps control how we behave.

text: Each hair grows out of a tiny pocket in your skin called a [[follicle|follicle]]. At the bottom of the follicle is a bulb of living cells that divide again and again. As new cells are made, they push the older ones up and out.

As those cells move up, they fill with a tough [[protein|protein]] called [[keratin|keratin]] and die. So the hair you can see and comb is dead. That's why a haircut doesn't hurt, while pulling a hair out by the root does.
Hair keeps you warm, protects your skin and eyes, and helps you feel things touching you.

st.prompt: You shave a patch of hair on your arm. When it grows back, it will be...
st.reveal: The same. Shaving cuts the hair off at the surface but doesn't touch the root, which decides how thick and dark it is. Regrowing hair can feel bristly because the cut end is blunt instead of tapered.

src: American Academy of Dermatology, hair loss and hair facts.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, hair.

d.try: Pull out one of the hairs left in your hairbrush and look at the end with a magnifying glass. If there's a tiny white bulb, that hair fell out naturally from its root. Then tape a hair onto dark paper next to a thread and compare their thickness.
myth: Shaving makes hair grow back thicker and darker.

Shaving only cuts the dead part of the hair. The root under the skin is untouched, so the hair grows back the same. It can look darker at first because short stubble hasn't been lightened by the sun yet.
facts: Hair roots on the whole body

sec.t:
Hair on your [[@gross-dandruff|scalp]] grows about 1 cm a month, around 15 cm a year. Each follicle works in cycles. It grows a hair for several years, rests for a few months, and then lets the old hair fall out as a new one starts underneath.

Because all your follicles are at different stages, you shed about 50 to 100 hairs a day without going bald. The growing stage decides how long your hair can get. In some people it lasts much longer, which is how a few people grow hair down to the floor.

Eyebrows steer [[@sweat|sweat]] and rain away from your eyes. Eyelashes catch dust and trigger a blink when something comes close. Nose hairs filter the air you breathe.

The hair on your head shades your scalp from the sun and helps keep it warm. Every hair also has nerves wrapped around its root, so it acts like a tiny feeler. That's how you can sense an ant on your arm before you see it.

When you're cold or scared, tiny muscles pull your hairs upright. You get [[@goosebumps|goosebumps]]. In furrier animals this traps a thicker layer of warm air, or makes the animal look bigger.

{{story:mammals-rise}}

Hair is one of the things that makes a [[mammal|mammal]] a mammal. Cats, elephants, whales and bats all have some. It may have helped early [[@mammals-rise|mammals]] stay warm at night while dinosaurs ruled the day.

Humans have about as many follicles as chimpanzees, but most of ours grow short, fine hairs. Scientists think losing thick fur may have helped our ancestors keep cool while walking and running in hot places, using sweat instead.

[[@hair-colour|Hair colour]] comes from [[melanin|melanin]], the same [[pigment|pigment]] that colours skin. Black and brown hair have lots of one kind. Red hair has more of another. As people get older, the colour-making cells slowly stop working, and new hairs grow in [[@grey-hair|grey]] or white.

Curly hair grows from oval or curved follicles. Straight hair grows from rounder ones. Your [[gene|genes]] decide which you have.

Hair matters in many cultures. In many Hindu families, a child's first haircut, called the *mundan*, is a ceremony. At the Tirumala temple in Andhra Pradesh, many pilgrims offer their hair as a sign of devotion, and the temple sells the hair to [[@oddity-history-hair|make wigs]]. Many Sikhs keep their hair uncut as part of their faith. Other [[@religions-world|religions]] have their own customs, from shaved heads to covered hair.

A hair pulled out by the root carries living cells, and those cells contain [[@dna|DNA]]. Forensic scientists can use it to help identify a person. A hair that simply fell out, or a cut piece, usually has much less DNA to work with, but it can still show things like whether someone dyed it.

text: In theory, yes. A space elevator would be a cable stretching from the [[equator|equator]] to more than 36,000 km above the Earth. Robot climbers would ride up and down it, carrying people and cargo to space without rockets.

The idea works because of a special height called geostationary [[orbit|orbit]], 35,786 km up. A satellite there circles the Earth exactly once a day, so it seems to hover over one spot. Fix a cable there, run it down to the ground and up beyond, add a heavy counterweight at the top, and Earth's spin keeps the whole thing pulled tight. The catch is the cable. No material we can make in long lengths is strong enough yet.

st.prompt: A climber rides a space elevator at 200 km/h, as fast as a fast train. How long to reach geostationary orbit, about 36,000 km up?
st.reveal: 36,000 ÷ 200 = 180 hours, or about seven and a half days. It is slow compared with a rocket, which reaches orbit in minutes, but it would need no rocket fuel at all.

src.NASA, Space elevators: an advanced Earth-space infrastructure for the new millennium (2000).

src: Arthur C. Clarke, The Fountains of Paradise (1979).
n.certNote: The physics of a space elevator is sound, but no known material can yet be made long and strong enough. Some engineers think it may be possible this century. Others think it may never be practical on Earth.

d.try: Tie a small soft toy to a piece of string about a metre long. Outdoors or in an open space, with nobody nearby, spin around slowly and feel the string pull tight. The toy is like the counterweight, and the string is like the cable. Spin faster and feel how much harder it pulls.
myth: A space elevator would be a super-tall tower built up from the ground.

No tower could hold its own weight that high. A space elevator would be a cable hanging down from a counterweight in space, kept tight because Earth's spin flings the counterweight outwards. It would be pulled, not squashed.

sec.h: A tower in a Russian dream
sec.t:
In 1895 the Russian scientist Konstantin Tsiolkovsky was inspired by the new [[@eiffel-tower|Eiffel Tower]] in Paris. He wondered what would happen if a tower kept going up and up. At the right height, he realised, anything on it would float, because it would be moving fast enough to stay in orbit.

In 1960 another Russian engineer, Yuri Artsutanov, flipped the idea around: hang a cable down from orbit instead of building up. In 1979 the science-fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke made it famous in his novel The Fountains of Paradise. He set it on an island called Taprobane, based on [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], where Clarke lived.

That tension is enormous. A steel cable long enough would snap under its own weight long before reaching orbit. Even the strongest fibres used in ropes and bulletproof vests are nowhere near good enough.

The best hope is carbon in special forms. Carbon nanotubes are tiny tubes of carbon [[atom|atoms]], and graphene is a sheet of carbon one atom thick. In the lab, they are many times stronger than steel for their weight. But scientists can only make them in short pieces, well under a metre long. A space elevator would need a flawless ribbon tens of thousands of kilometres long.

Even with the perfect cable, there'd be problems. Thousands of satellites and pieces of [[@space-junk|space junk]] cross the path, and any of them could cut it. Near the ground, storms, [[@lightning|lightning]] and strong winds would batter it. The cable would also need to be guarded, because damage anywhere along it could bring it down.

A Japanese construction company, Obayashi, has published plans for a space elevator by 2050, though it admits the material doesn't exist yet. Students and engineers hold contests to build robot climbers and test them on cables hanging from balloons and cranes.

Some scientists think a space elevator might be built first on the Moon, where [[gravity|gravity]] is weaker and existing materials might just be strong enough. For now, getting to space still means riding a rocket, though [[@reusable-rockets|reusable rockets]] have already made that much cheaper. A trip up the cable, if it ever happens, would be slow and quiet: about a week's ride, looking down at the Earth turning beneath you.

text: Every voice has a sound of its own, shaped by the size of your throat, your mouth and nose, your accent and how you speak. A voice-cloning program listens to recordings of a person and learns those patterns. Then it can make new speech in that voice, saying words the person never said.

Modern tools use AI that has already learned from thousands of hours of many people talking. So for a new voice, it may need only a short clip, sometimes just a few seconds, to copy the basic sound. Longer recordings make a better copy.
The same technology can give a voice back to someone who has lost theirs, or trick a grandparent into sending money to a scammer.

st.prompt: You get a call from a voice that sounds just like your uncle, saying he is in trouble and needs money now. What is the safest thing to do?

options.t: Hang up and call him back on the number you already have
Send the money quickly in case it is real
Ask him a question only he knows on the same call, then pay

st.reveal: A cloned voice can sound real, and scammers sometimes know personal details. Calling back on a number you trust, or asking an adult to do it, is the most reliable check. Many families also agree on a secret code word for emergencies.

d.try: Record yourself saying the same sentence three ways, happy, bored and scared, using a phone. Play them back to a family member and see if they can guess which is which. Your real voice carries feelings in tiny changes of speed and pitch, and that is part of what AI tries to copy.
myth: You can always tell a fake voice because it sounds robotic.

Old computer voices sounded flat and robotic, but modern clones can copy breathing, accents and emotion. Over a phone line, many people cannot tell the difference, which is why checking in other ways matters.
