sec.t:
People have tried to make machines talk for centuries. In 1939, at the New York World's Fair, Bell Labs showed off the Voder. A trained operator pressed keys and a foot pedal to produce buzzes and hisses shaped into words. It sounded strange and ghostly, but people could understand it.

Later computer voices pieced together tiny recorded sounds, which is why the voices of early sat-navs and talking toys sounded jumpy. In the 2010s, neural networks started producing much smoother speech. Today the voice of a phone assistant can sound almost like a real person reading aloud.

A cloning system first turns sound into a kind of picture of the voice, showing which pitches are loud and quiet over time. It studies how your voice rises and falls, how you say "s" and "r", and the little breaths between words.

The AI stores this as a set of numbers, a sort of voice fingerprint. Give it new text, and it builds speech one tiny slice at a time, matching that fingerprint. Some tools can even copy a voice in real time, changing your words into someone else's voice as you speak.

[[@voice|Your voice]] starts as a buzz from the vocal folds in your throat. The AI never sees your throat. It only copies the sound that comes out.

{{story:voice}}

For people with illnesses that take away their speech, such as motor neurone disease, cloning can be a gift. Before their voice fades, they record themselves reading for a while, a process called voice banking. Later, a computer can speak for them in something close to their own voice, instead of a stranger's.

Film studios use voice cloning to dub films into other languages in an actor's own voice. Audiobook makers use it too. Some uses are controversial, such as recreating the voices of performers who have died, and many actors and singers now ask for contracts that control how their voices can be used.

The darker side is fraud. Scammers take a short clip of someone from a video posted online, clone the voice, then phone a relative pretending there is an emergency: an accident, an arrest, a lost wallet abroad. They beg for money to be sent immediately. In 2023, the US Federal Trade Commission warned families about exactly this trick.

Fake voices have also been used to imitate politicians and company bosses. In 2024, US regulators ruled that robocalls using AI-generated voices were illegal without consent.

This is a close cousin of [[@deepfakes|deepfake]] video, where faces are swapped as well as voices.

The best defence is simple. If a call asks for money or secrets in a hurry, stop and check. Hang up and call the person back on a number you already know, or ask a parent to. Many families agree on a code word that a real relative would know and a scammer would not, a little like a spoken [[@passwords|password]].

Be careful about posting long videos of yourself talking publicly, especially with your full name. And if something feels wrong, tell a trusted adult. Good [[@online-safety|online safety]] habits work against fake voices as well as fake messages.

Meanwhile, researchers are building detectors that look for tiny clues a cloned voice leaves behind, patterns too faint for human ears. Similar AI is also used to make [[@tech-ai-music|music]], and some programs can now compose a whole song and sing it too.

text: A video game is a computer program, plus art, sound and a lot of careful design. Writers and designers decide what the game is about and what makes it fun. Artists draw characters and worlds. Sound designers and [[@video-game-music|composers]] make music and noises. [[@programming|Programmers]] write the code that ties it all together.

Then comes testing, and lots of it. People play unfinished versions again and again, looking for bugs, confusing bits and boring parts. A small phone game might take a few people a few months. A huge adventure game can take hundreds of people several years.

st.prompt: About how many times a second does a typical video game redraw the whole picture on your screen?
st.reveal: Most games draw between 30 and 60 complete pictures, called frames, every second. Each time, the game checks your buttons, moves everything a tiny bit and draws the scene again. Your eyes blend the frames into smooth movement.

d.try: Design a level on paper. Draw a simple map with a start, a goal, three obstacles and one secret. Then give it to a friend or family member to "play" by tracing a route with a finger while you explain the rules. Watch where they get stuck. That is exactly what game testers do.
myth: Video games are mostly played by children.
Surveys by the Entertainment Software Association find that the average American player is an adult in their thirties. In India too, millions of adults play games, mostly on their phones.

sec.t:
Few teams start from nothing. Most use a game engine, a big toolkit of ready-made code. An engine already knows how to draw 3D scenes, play sounds, make objects fall and bounce, and work on different machines. The team then adds its own world and rules on top.

Inside the game, characters are often moved by small programs. A guard in a stealth game might follow a simple rule: walk this path, and if you see the player, chase them. Clever games mix lots of simple rules like that, and players experience it as a character that seems to think.

Games also need physics, the rules for how things move. A ball must fall, bounce and roll in a way that feels right. Programmers write simple versions of real laws of motion, then often bend them. Many game characters can jump far higher than any athlete, because that is more fun.

sec.h: A tennis game in a lab
sec.t:
In 1958, a physicist named William Higinbotham worked at Brookhaven National Laboratory in New York. Each year the lab held a visitors' day, and he thought the displays were dull. So he wired up a lab screen to show a bouncing ball and a net, with two controllers. He called it [[@tennis|Tennis]] for Two. People queued to play it.

In 1972 the company Atari released Pong, a simple bat-and-ball game, in arcades across the United States. It was a giant hit and helped start the games industry. [[@tech-game-consoles|Home consoles]] that plugged into the [[@television-invented|family television]] soon followed. Early games had to fit into tiny amounts of memory, so their makers became experts at squeezing a whole world into a few simple shapes and beeps.

India now has its own game studios, and hundreds of millions of people in India play games, mostly on phones. Some Indian games draw on stories and settings from home, such as myths, cricket and city streets.

Many popular games also borrow from much older ones. [[@snakes-ladders|Snakes and ladders]], [[@carrom|carrom]] and [[@chess-india|chess]], which grew from the Indian game chaturanga, all have digital versions. A good game, old or new, still needs the same thing: rules that are simple to learn and hard to master.

text: Ancient Egyptians lived along the River Nile, a green ribbon of farmland running through the desert. Most were farmers who grew wheat, barley, flax and vegetables. They paid taxes in grain, believed in many gods, and were ruled by a king called the pharaoh.

Their [[civilisation|civilisation]] lasted about 3,000 years, longer than any modern country has existed. They built the [[@pyramids|pyramids]], wrote in [[@hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]], made paper from reeds, and prepared their dead carefully for a life after death.

st.prompt: Cleopatra died in 30 BCE. Did she live closer in time to the building of the Great Pyramid, or to the first Moon landing?

options.t: The building of the Great Pyramid
About the same distance from both

st.reveal: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BCE, about 2,500 years before Cleopatra. The Moon landing in 1969 came about 2,000 years after her. Ancient Egypt lasted so long that, to Cleopatra, the pyramids were already ancient.

sec.t:
Most Egyptians lived in [[@cave-to-houses|mud-brick houses]] with flat roofs, where families slept on hot nights. They ate [[@wheat-bread|bread]], onions, lentils, fish and fruit such as dates and figs. They drank a thick, mild beer made from barley, which was also used to pay workers.

People wore light linen clothes made from flax. Men and women both wore eye makeup, called kohl, which may also have helped protect against the glare of the sun and eye [[infection|infections]]. Children played with balls, spinning tops and wooden toys, and adults played [[@sport-ancient-games|board games like senet]].

Animals were everywhere. [[@cats-domestic|Cats]] kept mice away from grain stores and were linked with the goddess Bastet. Some families kept dogs, monkeys and even geese as [[@pets-care|pets]].

One of the best views of everyday life comes from Deir el-Medina, a village near Thebes, now Luxor. The skilled workers who carved and painted royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings lived there with their families for hundreds of years.

They wrote notes on broken pottery and flakes of stone, and thousands survive. They record sick days, arguments, shopping, lessons and love poems. One worker missed work because a scorpion stung him. Another stayed home to brew beer. Around 1150 BCE, when their grain rations were late, the workers stopped work and sat down outside temples until they were paid.

Egyptian women had more rights than in many ancient societies. They could own land, run businesses, sign contracts and go to court. A few women ruled as pharaoh. Hatshepsut reigned for about 20 years and sent a trading [[expedition|expedition]] to a land called Punt, bringing back incense trees.

[[@myths-egyptian|Egyptians believed in hundreds of gods]], such as Ra the sun god and Osiris, ruler of the dead. The pharaoh was seen as a link between the gods and the people. They believed that after death, a person's heart was weighed against a feather. A good life meant a happy afterlife in a land like Egypt, only better.

That belief is why they made [[@mummies|mummies]] and filled tombs with food, furniture, games and little figures of servants. Much of what we know about daily life comes from these tombs.

Scribes wrote on papyrus, a paper-like sheet made from reeds that grew along the Nile. Being a scribe was a respected job, and boys trained for years. Papyrus was so useful that it was traded across the Mediterranean. Our word "paper" comes from it, even though true [[@paper-invention|paper]] was invented later, in China.

text: The first cities grew in places where farming produced more food than farmers needed. That spare food meant some people could do other jobs full time: making pots, trading, building, writing records or leading worship. Thousands of people living close together needed walls, streets, water, drains and rules.

Which was the very first city depends on what you call a city. [[@cave-to-houses|Çatalhöyük]] in Turkey was a large town about 9,000 years ago. [[@sumer|Uruk]], in Mesopotamia, grew into what many historians call the first true city around 5,000 years ago. Soon after, cities rose along [[@egypt-nile|the Nile]], the Indus, the Yellow River and, separately, in Peru.

st.prompt: How did people get into their houses in Çatalhöyük, about 9,000 years ago?

options.t: Through a hole in the roof, by ladder
Through front doors on wide streets

st.reveal: The mud-brick houses were packed wall to wall with no streets between them. People walked across the flat rooftops and climbed down a wooden ladder through an opening that also let out smoke from the oven.

n.certNote: Experts disagree about what counts as a city rather than a large village, so the "first city" depends on the definition. Population numbers for ancient cities are estimates.

Many did, but not all. In the Indus cities, archaeologists have found big public buildings, granaries and a huge bath, but no clear palace or royal tombs. How these cities were run is still a mystery.

sec.t:
Çatalhöyük was home to perhaps several thousand people from about 7100 BCE. Its mud-brick houses were packed so tightly that people moved around on the roofs. Inside, families slept on raised platforms, cooked at ovens, and painted walls with hunting scenes. They buried their dead under the floors.

Many experts call it a big village or town rather than a city. Nearly every house looked alike, and there are few signs of rich and poor, rulers or specialists.

Around 2600 BCE, cities appeared in the Indus valley, in today's Pakistan and north-west India. Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were laid out on a grid, with main streets running north to south and east to west. Houses were built of baked bricks of standard sizes. Many had bathrooms connected to covered drains, cleaner than many cities had thousands of years later.

The [[@indus-cities|Indus cities]] stretched far. Dholavira in Gujarat, on an island in the [[@earth-salt-flats|salt flats]] of Kutch, had huge water tanks to catch rain. It became a UNESCO [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] Site in 2021. Rakhigarhi in Haryana may have been one of the largest of all.

Egypt's cities grew along the Nile. In China, early cities rose along the Yellow River. In Peru, Caral was built around 2600 BCE, with stepped pyramids and sunken plazas, without any contact with Asia or Africa. People in different places invented cities on their own.

In 1950 the [[archaeologist|archaeologist]] V. Gordon Childe listed signs of a true city, such as full-time specialists, large public buildings, trade, writing and a surplus of food. Not every early city had all of them, which is why the debate continues.

Cities brought new inventions and ideas, as crowds of people swapped skills. They also brought new problems: rubbish, disease, crime and the need to share water. Today more than half of all people live in cities, and planners still wrestle with the same questions the builders of Mohenjo-daro faced: where [[@water-purify|clean water]] comes from and where [[@toilets-sewers|waste goes]].

text: Historians find out about the past by studying sources: anything that gives evidence about what happened. These include letters, [[@diaries|diaries]], laws, newspapers, coins, [[inscription|inscriptions]], photographs, buildings and people's memories.

Then they ask hard questions. Who made this source? When, and why? Were they there? Did they have a reason to exaggerate or hide something? A single source is never enough, so historians compare many sources to see where they agree. Where the evidence is thin, good historians say so. History is less a list of facts than a careful argument built on evidence.

st.prompt: Two letters describe the same battle. One was written by a soldier the next day. The other was written by a general's son 40 years later. Which is the primary source?
st.reveal: The soldier was there, so his letter is a primary source. It still needs checking, because he saw only one corner of the battle and may have had reasons to boast. The later letter is a secondary source, useful in other ways.

d.try: Ask two people in your family to describe the same event, like a wedding or a trip, separately. Write down what each says. Compare the stories and list where they agree and where they differ. You've just done what historians do every day.
myth: Vikings wore helmets with horns.

No Viking-age helmet with horns has been found. The idea became popular in the 1800s, helped by costume designs for an 1876 opera by Richard Wagner. The one well-preserved Viking helmet ever found has no horns.
facts: made at the time, by people who were there
written later, by people studying the past

sec.t:
A primary source comes from the time being studied. A diary written during a war, a king's coin or a photo of a protest are primary sources. A secondary source is written later by someone studying the past, like a textbook or this article.

Primary sources are closer to events but can be narrow or biased. A secondary source can see the bigger picture but depends on how well its author used the evidence.

Kings often carved records of their victories. They rarely mentioned their defeats. Historians call this bias, when a source leans one way. Bias doesn't make a source useless, but it means reading it carefully.

Some sources survive only in pieces. The Greek visitor Megasthenes wrote a book about India around 300 BCE, in the time of the [[@mauryan-empire|Mauryan empire]]. The book is lost. We know parts of it only because later writers quoted it, and they may have changed things.

Others are surprisingly honest. The Mughal emperor Babur wrote a memoir, the *Baburnama*, describing his mistakes, his homesickness and the fruits he missed from Central Asia.

Sometimes a source exists, but nobody can read it. For centuries, the [[edict|edicts]] of Emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]], carved on rocks and pillars across India, were a mystery, because the Brahmi script had been forgotten. In 1837, James Prinsep, an official at the Calcutta mint, worked it out. Suddenly a great emperor's own words could be heard again.

In Egypt, the Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, carried the same text in three scripts, including [[@hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]] and Greek. Using the Greek as a key, Jean-François Champollion announced in 1822 that he could read [[hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]].

History changes as new evidence appears and new people ask questions. For a long time, history books focused on kings and generals. Today historians also study farmers, women, children, workers and enslaved people, using sources such as songs, recipes, court records and oral histories, the memories people tell aloud.

Old beliefs get corrected. Many people still picture [[@vikings|Vikings]] in horned helmets, but the evidence says otherwise. A good historian is always ready to say "we used to think this, but now the evidence shows something else."

text: Shivaji Bhonsle was a Maratha leader who founded an independent kingdom in western India in the 17th century. He was born in 1630 at Shivneri fort, near [[@pune|Pune]].

At the time, most of the Deccan was ruled by the [[@india-wonder-gol-gumbaz|Sultanate of Bijapur]] and the mighty [[@mughals|Mughal Empire]]. Starting as a teenager with a small band of followers, Shivaji captured hill forts in the Sahyadri mountains, also called the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]]. He used fast raids, local knowledge and surprise to beat much bigger armies. In 1674 he was crowned king at Raigad, taking the title Chhatrapati. He built a navy, ran an organised government and is a hero across Maharashtra and beyond.

st.reveal: Sindhudurg, built in the 1660s, stands on a small island off the Konkan coast. It guarded the coast and the trade routes and kept enemy fleets at a distance. Sea forts like this were part of Shivaji's plan to build Maratha power at sea.

myth: Shivaji fought the Mughals because he hated Muslims.

He fought the Mughal emperor and the sultans of Bijapur for land and power. Muslims served as officers in his army and navy, and even Mughal historians wrote that he ordered his soldiers not to harm mosques or holy books.

sec.t:
Shivaji's father, Shahaji, was a general who served the Bijapur sultans and spent long years away. Shivaji grew up in Pune with his mother, Jijabai. She told him stories from the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]] and is remembered as the strongest influence on his life.

Around 1645, while still in his teens, Shivaji and his companions captured Torna fort. Soon he held a chain of forts across the hills. The local hillmen, called Mavalas, knew every path and became his soldiers.

sec.h: Tiger claws and a surprise at night

sec.t:
In 1665, after a Mughal army besieged his forts, Shivaji signed a [[treaty|treaty]] and handed over many of them. The next year he visited the emperor Aurangzeb's court in Agra, where he felt insulted and was placed under guard.

According to the famous story, he escaped by hiding in large baskets of sweets being sent out of the house. However he did it, he got back to Maharashtra, won back his forts and grew stronger than before.

In 1674, at Raigad, Shivaji was crowned in a grand ceremony. He set up a council of eight ministers, used [[@marathi-gujarati|Marathi]] in government and had a dictionary made to replace Persian words with [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] and Marathi ones.

He also saw that power on the Konkan coast needed ships. He built a fleet and sea forts, including Sindhudurg on an island off the coast. Because of this, he is often called the father of the Indian Navy. In 2022 the Indian Navy adopted a new flag with a design inspired by his royal seal.

Shivaji is said to have held or built more than 300 forts, many perched on cliffs that disappear into [[@monsoon|monsoon]] clouds for months. They had water cisterns cut into rock, winding gateways to slow attackers and hidden escape routes. Unlike the stone [[@knights-castles|castles]] of Europe, which often stood on flat ground, these forts used the cliffs themselves as walls.

In 2025, UNESCO listed twelve forts as the Maratha Military Landscapes of India, including Shivneri, Raigad, Pratapgad and Sindhudurg, and Gingee in Tamil Nadu. Shivaji died at Raigad in 1680. The Maratha power he started kept growing and later stretched from Tamil Nadu to Punjab.

text: From north to south, India is a land of giant steps. At the top are the Himalaya, the highest mountains on Earth. Below them lie the wide, flat plains of [[@rivers-himalaya|the Ganga]] and Brahmaputra rivers, among the most crowded and [[fertile|fertile]] places in the world.

To the west is the [[@desert-life|Thar Desert]]. In the middle and south rises the Deccan Plateau, a huge raised table of old rock, edged by two ranges of hills called the Western and Eastern Ghats. Around it all runs a long coastline, ending at [[@kanyakumari|Kanyakumari]], where three seas meet.
India covers about 32.9 lakh km², the seventh largest country. Two groups of islands, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and [[@lakshadweep|Lakshadweep]], add even more variety.

st.reveal: Kanyakumari is the southern tip of mainland India. But Indira Point, on Great Nicobar Island in the Bay of Bengal, lies even further south, only about 6.75 degrees north of the equator.

Everest stands on the border of Nepal and China. India's highest mountain is Kangchenjunga, 8,586 m, on the border of Sikkim and Nepal. It is the third highest mountain on Earth.

sec.t:
The [[@himalaya-form|Himalaya]] form India's northern wall, stretching about 2,400 km. They began rising about 5 crore years ago, when India collided with Asia. Kangchenjunga, India's highest peak, reaches 8,586 m.

The mountains do two big jobs. They block icy winds from Central Asia, keeping northern India warmer. And their [[glacier|glaciers]] and snow feed great rivers like the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra. Beyond them lies Ladakh, a high, cold desert where it hardly rains.

In the west, the [[@thar-formed|Thar Desert]] covers much of Rajasthan, with sand dunes, thorny scrub and very little rain.

The [[@deccan|Deccan]] Plateau fills most of southern India. Much of its western part is made of black [[basalt|basalt]] rock, from enormous [[lava|lava]] floods about 6.6 crore years ago, around the time the dinosaurs died out. Its rivers, such as the Godavari and Krishna, flow east towards the Bay of Bengal, because the plateau tilts that way.

The Western Ghats catch the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] rains, making the west coast and Kerala lush and green. Low areas like Kuttanad even lie below sea level. Far to the north-east, [[@meghalaya|Mawsynram]] in Meghalaya is one of the wettest places on Earth.

India's coastline was long measured at about 7,500 km. A new survey using more detailed maps, published in 2024, put it at more than 11,000 km, because it counted many more bends and inlets.

India shares land borders with Pakistan, [[@china-today|China]], Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar. Sri Lanka lies just across a narrow stretch of sea called the Palk Strait, and the [[@maldives|Maldives]] sits to the south-west.

Inside, India is divided into states and union [[territory|territories]], each with its own landscape. Rajasthan is the biggest state by area. Goa is the smallest.

India stretches about 2,900 km from west to east. In Arunachal Pradesh, the Sun rises roughly two hours earlier than in western Gujarat. Yet the whole country runs on one clock, Indian Standard Time. Some people in the north-east have asked for a separate time zone, a question still being discussed.

text: The Kumbh Mela is a Hindu [[pilgrimage|pilgrimage]] where people come to bathe in sacred rivers, believing a dip at the right time washes away sins. It rotates between four cities: Prayagraj, Haridwar, Nashik and Ujjain. The biggest, the Maha Kumbh at Prayagraj, drew enormous crowds from 13 January to 26 February 2025.

Organising it is like building a city in a few months. The Ganga and Yamuna meet at Prayagraj. On their sandy banks, the Uttar Pradesh government and many agencies laid out about 4,000 hectares in 25 sectors, with roads, bridges, power lines, water pipes, hospitals, police stations and tents. When the mela ended, almost all of it came down again.

st.prompt: How do pilgrims cross the Ganga at the Kumbh Mela in Prayagraj?

options.t: On temporary bridges built on floating steel pontoons

st.reveal: Engineers float hollow steel pontoons on the river and lay roads across them. In 2025 about 30 of these bridges were planned, built from more than 3,000 pontoons, and taken apart again afterwards.

d.try: Plan a pretend mela for your school. On a sheet of paper, mark where people will enter, where the toilets, water taps, first-aid tents and lost-and-found desk will go, and how people will walk in and out without bumping into each other. Then show it to a friend and ask them to spot the problem areas.
myth: The Kumbh Mela happens in the same place every year.
It moves between four cities. Each site hosts a full Kumbh roughly every 12 years, with smaller gatherings in between, and the dates are set by the positions of Jupiter, the Sun and the Moon.
facts: listed as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2017

sec.t:
How do you count tens of crores of people? Organisers used cameras, drones, train and bus records and even software that estimates crowd size from images. The official total for 2025 was over 66 crore visits, around half of India's population.

Not everyone accepts that number. Some journalists and researchers argue that the methods count the same people many times, or overestimate crowds. What is clear is that on the biggest bathing days, crowds ran into crores, among the largest human gatherings ever recorded.

Hindu tradition tells of gods and demons churning the ocean to find amrit, the [[nectar|nectar]] of immortality. As it was carried away in a pot, or kumbh, four drops fell to Earth. They landed at the four Kumbh sites.

The date of each mela depends on astrology, the positions of Jupiter, the Sun and the Moon. That is why the gaps between gatherings are not always exactly equal. The next full Kumbh is the Simhastha at Nashik and Trimbakeshwar, expected in 2027, followed by Ujjain.

Some of the most famous sights are the processions of akharas, orders of sadhus (holy men), many of them ash-covered, who lead the first baths on the most important days. People also come to camp for a whole month, living simply, praying and listening to teachers.

With so many people, getting lost is easy. "Lost and found" centres, called khoya-paya kendras, have been part of the mela for decades. In 2025 there were ten digital centres that registered missing people and announced names on loudspeakers across the site.

Huge crowds can be dangerous. On 29 January 2025, one of the busiest bathing days, a crowd crush near the Sangam killed at least 30 people according to official figures. Journalists later reported that the true number was higher. Each such tragedy leads to new rules about how crowds should be guided and spread out.

Satellites have photographed the Kumbh, showing the tent city as a vast grid on the riverbank. Other pilgrimages, such as the [[@mecca-hajj|Hajj in Mecca]], face many of the same puzzles of water, shade and crowd flow. And the river at the centre of it all has a journey of its own, from a Himalayan [[glacier|glacier]] to the Bay of Bengal, traced in the [[@ganga-journey|journey of the Ganga]].

text: The [[@golden-gate|Golden Gate Bridge]] is orange because an architect named Irving Morrow loved the colour. When the steel arrived, it was coated in a reddish-orange primer, the first layer of paint that protects metal from [[@rust|rust]]. Morrow thought it looked beautiful against the brown hills, blue sea and grey fog. It was also easy to see.

Others had different ideas. The US Navy wanted black and yellow stripes so ships could spot it, and some suggested plain grey or silver. Morrow won, and the bridge was painted a shade now called International Orange. It opened in May 1937.

st.prompt: Why was the Golden Gate Bridge painted orange?

options.t: It looks good against the hills and stands out in fog

sec.t:
The Golden Gate is a narrow strait, about 1.6 km wide, where San Francisco Bay meets the Pacific Ocean. The explorer John C. Frémont named it Chrysopylae, or Golden Gate, in about 1846, comparing it to a harbour in Istanbul. That was before [[@gold-rush|gold was found in California]] and long before the bridge.

For years, people said a bridge here was impossible. The water is deep, the currents are strong, winds are fierce and fog rolls in almost daily. Engineer Joseph Strauss led the project, and Charles Ellis and Leon Moisseiff did much of the hard maths behind the design.

San Francisco's famous fog comes from the sea. A cold [[@ocean-currents|ocean current]] runs down the California coast, and deep cold water rises near the shore. When warm, damp air blows over that cold water, it cools and turns into fog. In summer, the fog often pours through the Golden Gate in the afternoon. People in the city have even given it a nickname, Karl.

San Francisco sits close to the San Andreas Fault, where two huge plates of Earth's crust slide past each other. Early on 18 April 1906, a powerful [[@earthquakes|earthquake]] struck. Fires broke out across the city and burned for days. Much of San Francisco was destroyed, and thousands died. Today buildings and bridges are built to sway and survive shaking.

sec.h: Gold, cable cars and new ideas
sec.t:
In 1848, [[@gold-where|gold]] was found in the hills east of the city. San Francisco grew from a village of about 1,000 people to a busy city of about 25,000 in a couple of years. Workers came from across the world, including from [[@china-today|China]]. The city's Chinatown is one of the oldest in North America.

San Francisco's hills are so steep that horses struggled to pull carts up them. In 1873, Andrew Hallidie started cable cars, pulled along by a moving cable under the street. They still run, and they are the last cable cars of their kind in the world still worked by hand.

text: The Suez Canal is a 193 km channel of seawater across Egypt. It joins the Mediterranean Sea in the north to the Red Sea in the south. Ships sailing between Asia and Europe can use it instead of going all the way around Africa.

For a voyage between Mumbai and London, that saves thousands of kilometres and well over a week at sea. Before the trouble that began in late 2023, more than 20,000 ships a year used the canal, often said to carry about 12% of the world's trade. Oil, cars, clothes, phones and grain all pass through it. When the canal is blocked, shops and factories on the other side of the world can feel it within weeks.

st.reveal: Strong winds pushed the 400 m ship into the bank. Diggers and dredgers scooped out sand from around its bow, tugboats pulled, and an especially high tide helped float it free on 29 March. By then hundreds of ships were waiting.

sec.h: A short cut through the desert
sec.t:
People had dreamed of joining these seas for thousands of years. Ancient [[@ancient-egypt|Egyptian]] rulers dug canals linking the Nile to the Red Sea, but they silted up and were abandoned.

The modern canal was built by a French-led company under Ferdinand de Lesseps, starting in 1859. In the early years, huge numbers of Egyptian peasants were forced to dig, often by hand, in brutal heat. Many died, though nobody knows exactly how many. Later, steam-powered dredgers did much of the work. The canal opened on 17 November 1869 with fireworks and a grand parade of ships.

The Suez Canal is simpler than the [[@panama-canal|Panama Canal]]. The two seas are at almost the same level, and the land between is low desert, so there is no need to lift ships. The canal also passes through some lakes along the way.

Ships travel in convoys, one behind another, guided by Egyptian pilots who know every bend. Parts of the canal allow only one-way traffic, so convoys take turns. In 2015 Egypt opened a new parallel channel along part of the route so more ships could pass in both directions.

The canal changed travel between Europe and India. Before 1869, sailing ships from Britain took months to reach Bombay around Africa. Through Suez, steamships could do it in a few weeks. Bombay's port boomed, and [[@mumbai|Mumbai]] grew into India's great trading city. Cotton, tea and indigo flowed out, and British goods and officials flowed in.

{{story:trade-world}}

In March 2021, strong winds pushed the Ever Given, a container ship about 400 m long, sideways across the canal. Its bow was wedged in one bank and its stern near the other. For six days nothing could pass. Diggers and dredgers scooped sand from around the bow, and tugboats, helped by a high tide, pulled it free on 29 March. By then hundreds of ships were waiting.

In 1956, Egypt's president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, took control of the canal from the company that ran it. Britain, France and Israel then invaded. Under pressure from the USA, the Soviet Union and the United Nations, they withdrew. The UN sent one of its first [[@peacekeepers|peacekeeping]] forces to the area.

After a war in 1967, the canal was closed for eight years. Fifteen ships were trapped in one of its lakes the whole time. Their crews, from many countries, visited each other, held a sailing contest and printed their own stamps.

Since late 2023, attacks on ships in the Red Sea led many shipping companies to avoid the area and sail around Africa instead. Traffic through the canal fell sharply, and Egypt lost billions of dollars in fees. In late 2025 and early 2026, some of the big shipping lines began cautiously sending ships back through. Some soon switched back to the long route around Africa when the risks rose again. A narrow ribbon of water in the desert still decides how fast much of the world gets its goods.

text: Rabindranath Tagore was a [[@bengali-language|Bengali]] poet, writer, composer, painter and teacher. He was born in Calcutta, now [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], in 1861, and died there in 1941. People often call him Gurudev, meaning "respected teacher".

In 1913 he became the first person from outside Europe to win the [[@nobel-literature|Nobel Prize in Literature]], for a book of poems called Gitanjali, "Song Offerings". He wrote the words and music of India's national anthem, Jana Gana Mana, and also of [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]]'s anthem, Amar Shonar Bangla. He wrote poems, novels, short stories, plays and essays, and he started a school that is still running.

It was first sung at a Congress meeting in Calcutta in 1911, during the king's visit to India, and some newspapers linked the two. Tagore later wrote that the "lord of destiny" in the song was not any king. Most historians accept his explanation.

sec.t:
Tagore was the youngest of thirteen surviving children in a wealthy family at Jorasanko in north Calcutta. The house was always busy with music, plays, magazines and debates. His family took part in the [[@bengali-renaissance|Bengal Renaissance]], a time of new thinking about religion, education and society. His father, Debendranath, was a religious reformer. One elder brother, Satyendranath, became the first Indian to join the Indian Civil Service.

He hated school. He found the classrooms dull and the teaching harsh, and he left several schools. He was taught mostly at home, and he wrote his first poems as a child. Later he studied briefly in England but returned without a degree.

Gitanjali was first published in Bengali in 1910. On a trip to England in 1912, Tagore translated some of the poems into English himself. He showed them to the painter William Rothenstein, who passed them to the Irish poet W. B. Yeats. Yeats was so moved that he wrote an introduction for the English edition.

Within a year, the book had won the Nobel Prize. One of its poems, which begins "Where the mind is without fear", is still recited in Indian schools. It describes a free country where knowledge is open to all.

In 1901 Tagore started a small school at Santiniketan, about 150 km north of Calcutta. Many lessons were held outdoors, under trees, with music, art and nature as part of learning. In 1921 it grew into Visva-Bharati University, meant to bring together ideas from India and the rest of the world.

Famous students include the filmmaker [[@satyajit-ray|Satyajit Ray]] and [[@indira-gandhi|Indira Gandhi]]. In 2023, Santiniketan was added to UNESCO's [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] list.

Tagore supported India's [[@freedom-struggle|freedom struggle]], though he sometimes disagreed with Gandhi about how to win it. The two men argued in public and respected each other deeply.

The British government knighted him in 1915. In 1919, after soldiers fired on an unarmed crowd at [[@jallianwala|Jallianwala Bagh]] in Amritsar, he gave up the knighthood in protest. He wrote to the Viceroy that he wanted to stand beside his fellow Indians.

He travelled widely and met scientists and writers, including Albert [[@einstein|Einstein]] in 1930. Their recorded conversation about truth and beauty is still read today. Every morning, millions of schoolchildren in India and Bangladesh begin the day singing his words as their [[@anthems|anthems]].

text: The samosa came to India from Central Asia and the Middle East. Over a thousand years ago, cooks in Persia and the Arab world made small pastries filled with minced meat, called sanbusak or sanbusaj. In Central Asia, a baked version called samsa was popular.

Traders, soldiers and cooks travelling along the old routes into India carried the recipe with them. By the 1200s and 1300s, samosas were being served at the courts of the [[@delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]]. Back then they were stuffed with meat and nuts. The potato samosa, now the most common kind, came centuries later.

myth: The samosa was invented in India.
The samosa's ancestors were made in Central Asia and the Middle East. Cooks and traders brought them to India around the 1200s or 1300s. India gave the samosa its potato filling and made it famous.

sec.t:
Small, sealed pastries made sense for people on the move. They could be cooked over a campfire, carried in a saddlebag and eaten without plates. Traders crossing deserts and mountains along routes such as the [[@silk-road|Silk Road]] took them along.

Arabic cookbooks from the 10th to 13th centuries describe sanbusaj, filled with meat and fried in oil. The name changed as it travelled. It became sambusa in Persia, samsa in Central Asia, and samosa or sambusa in India.

Potatoes reached India from South America in the 1600s, brought by Portuguese traders. They took time to become popular. Once they did, the potato samosa took off.

Potatoes were cheaper than meat, and a filling of spiced potato and peas suited the many vegetarians in India. Today the potato samosa, eaten with green chutney or [[@tamarind|tamarind]] sauce, is sold at tea stalls, railway stations and sweet shops across the country.

A samosa is usually a [[@geometry-everyday|triangle]] or a cone. Cooks fold a strip or half-circle of dough into a cone, fill it and seal the open edge. The pointed shape holds the filling tightly and helps the pastry fry evenly.

Triangles are strong shapes that don't bend easily, which you can read about in [[@shapes-angles|shapes and angles]]. A samosa with a well-sealed seam won't burst in the hot oil.

The samosa's family is still spread far and wide. In Bengal, a smaller version is called singara. In East Africa, sambusas are made with meat or [[@lentils-world|lentils]]. In Portugal and Goa, a similar pastry is called chamuça. Central Asian samsa is baked in a clay oven, not fried.

Indians who moved to Britain, the USA and Canada took the samosa with them, and it's now sold in supermarkets from London to Toronto. During Ramadan, samosas are a favourite food to break the fast in many countries, from Pakistan to Somalia. A triangle of pastry has crossed more borders than most travellers.

In India, the samosa is the classic snack with afternoon [[@food-chai-history|chai]]. It's served at birthday parties, office meetings and cricket matches. It turns up as [[@food-street-food-world|street food]] in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]] and [[@kolkata|Kolkata]] alike. Sweet shops in some places even make sweet samosas filled with khoa or dried fruit.

text: Fizzy drinks are fizzy because of [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]], the same gas you breathe out. At the factory, the gas is forced into cold, sweetened water under high pressure, and the bottle is sealed fast. Under that pressure, far more gas [[dissolve|dissolves]] in the liquid than it normally could.

When you open the bottle, you hear a hiss: that is the pressure escaping. Now the liquid holds more gas than it can keep, so the extra gas slowly comes out as bubbles. Some of the carbon dioxide also forms a weak [[acid|acid]] in the water, called carbonic acid. It gives soda water its sharp, slightly tingly taste on the tongue.

st.prompt: You open two bottles of the same soda, one from the fridge and one that sat in the sun. Which one fizzes over more?
st.reveal: Cold water can hold more dissolved gas than warm water. In a warm bottle, more carbon dioxide is ready to escape the moment the pressure drops, so it rushes out in a foamy burst.

sec.t:
Gas dissolves better in liquid when it is pushed in hard, and when the liquid is cold. Scientists describe this with a rule called Henry's law. A sealed bottle of cola is under several times the normal air [[pressure|pressure]], a bit like a car tyre.

Bubbles need a place to start. They form on tiny scratches, specks of dust or rough surfaces, which scientists call nucleation sites. That is why bubbles rise in streams from the same spots on the side of a glass, and why dropping certain [[@candy-history|sweets]] into a bottle of soda can make it foam out.

sec.h: A scientist next to a brewery

sec.t:
In the 1800s, soda water was thought to be good for health and was sold in American pharmacies, with flavoured syrups mixed in at a counter called a soda fountain. In 1886, a pharmacist named John Pemberton created Coca-Cola in Atlanta, Georgia. Pepsi followed in 1893 in North Carolina.

Bottling made these drinks travel. By the middle of the 20th century, American colas were sold in almost every country, helped by enormous [[@advertising|advertising]] budgets.

In 1977, Coca-Cola stopped selling in India after a dispute over new government rules for foreign companies. Indian firms filled the gap. Parle launched Thums Up, a strong, spicy cola, to sit beside its orange Gold Spot and lemony Limca. When Coca-Cola returned in 1993, it bought these brands, and Thums Up is still one of the best-selling soft drinks in India.

Long before big brands, there was goli soda. Its thick glass bottle, called a Codd-neck bottle after the Englishman Hiram Codd who patented it in 1872, has a marble trapped in its neck. The gas pushes the marble up against a rubber seal. To open it, the seller presses the marble down with a pop, a sound that many Indian adults still connect with summer holidays.

A regular 330 ml can of cola contains about 35 g of [[@sugar|sugar]], roughly seven teaspoons. The cold temperature and the acid make that sweetness taste less strong than it really is. Sugary, acidic sips through the day are hard on [[@sugar-teeth|teeth]], so health experts suggest keeping these drinks as an occasional treat, and the bubbles are just as fizzy in plain soda water.
